He is the peripatetic minister; he is never around when I want to ask him a question.
However, there has been circulating quite widely in Canada, and it came to my attention when I was in British Columbia recently, a document which is said to be a cabinet document making certain recommendations concerning revisions to the Indian Act. To quote from this document it says:
The following proposals for a revised Indian Act revolve around two basic themes-
And one of these themes in the document is that the band should have:
powers and jurisdiction over the on-reserve management and utilization of fish and game
That does not say whether it is just for their own use, which is a treaty right which allows no exception and is perfectly in order, or whether it goes on for commercial purposes. The way that this was to be done was to revise section 88 of the Indian Act. Here we run across a fifth minister. Section 88 provides that the Indians are subject to provincial legislation, but the revisions are intended to provide that the Indians on the reserve should be subject to federal legislation as well, unless parliament expressly provides otherwise. So there is a real hodgepodge here. We are moving over into the field of federal-provincial relations. We now have the Minister of Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Lalonde) involved. That is now five ministers that this apparently innocuous act of the Minister of Indian Affairs involved. I am surprised at all this but I suppose they have to put up a brave face.
The ministers concerned show little concern about the implications of what they are doing. There is the Minister of Fisheries, some of whose management jurisdiction has been taken away; then the Minister of the Environment, because some of his juridiction will be taken away, and, by implication, that brings in the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) because of the international tangents, and finally the Minister of Federal-Provincial Relations because of the proposed amendments to section 88.
From this memoradum I referred to before, let me quote the following:
Where treaties are silent about government regulation-

That is, treaties with the Indian Tribes. The article continues:
Such laws would appear not to apply to the Indian people entitled to the benefits of these treaties. Accordingly the Migratory Birds Convention Act would not apply to them and Canada would effectively be in breach of international convention-
This is a memorandum by the public servants to their minister about proposals that they are making to put Canada in breach of international conventions. I do not know what has happened to public servants when they come forward with this notion.
This memorandum goes on to say:
While the Migratory Birds Convention Act and the federal Fisheries Act are federal legislation, they deal with areas which the provinces consider to be otherwise within their jurisdiction in the sense that they form part of the natural resources of the province.
As I say, that is how this problem has overflowed into the area of federal-provincial relations.
I suspect there is one further area which is beyond the powers of this legislature in that these matters may come before the courts to be resolved. The memorandum states that: The courts have not settled the question of the full effect of the Natural Resources Transfer Agreements on the prairie treaties.
Are the resources that were affected by the transfer agreements superseded by the treaties or do the treaties take over from there?
The memorandum goes on to say:
It is proposed that the revised Indian Act provide clear authority to Bands to make bylaws concerning the management and use of fish and game resources within the boundaries of reserves and clear powers to enforce such bylaws.
There is surely a ground for compromise here which was not envisaged and which ought to be envisaged. The treaty commitments have to be honoured. There is no question about that, but to accord even within the reserves over-all, complete, entire and unique jurisdiction in those areas that are of federal or provincial concern is merely to cause greater problems than we already have, when goodness knows we have enough problems without this one.
The suggestion is made in the memorandum that there might be Indian participation on local game advisory boards. That is fine. Perhaps that would be a better way of doing it so that there might be Indian participation on the advisory boards and the band members might become game enforcement officers on the reserves. Sure, why not? But to extend this, what is called a right, to the Indians, and then to suggest that having done so it might be possible to encourage them to enter agreements either with the province with respect to game or with the federal authorities with respect to fish is, I am sure, asking a bit too much.
I would suggest that the Indian Act as it now stands does have within it, in section 60 and section 73, the power to resolve this matter. As is usual, the resolution suggesting positive steps comes from this side of the House. Do not be surprised if within the next month or so this dispute has been resolved. Full credit will be taken by the ministers concerned. However, let it be noted that here today I mention that
October 30, 1978

sections 60 and 73 contain within them a germ of a solution to this problem.
Section 60( 1) reads as follows:
The governor in council may at the request of a band grant to the band the right to exercise such control and management over lands in the reserve-
We have the granting of a right. 1 question the use of the word "right" because section 60(2) reads:
The governor in council may ai any time withdraw from a band a right conferred upon the band under subsection (1).
I wonder if "right" is the correct word to use. Is it not a privilege, authority, or power? The word "right" has gathered around it a sanctity which, once given, is very difficult to withdraw, although it states quite clearly the so-called right may be withdrawn.
We ran into this problem last week when talking about the right to strike in the Post Office. It had been granted by parliament, and withdrawn on that occasion. Therefore I wonder if we are using the right terminology here.
I mentioned that section 73 would facilitate the resolution of this argument. That section reads as follows:
The governor in council may make regulations for the protection and preservation of fur-bearing animals, fish and other game on reserves;
I think there is groundwork here. Having exposed the dispute, it is obviously there. However, very little is being said about it. When one minister says on the floor of the House that another minister goofed, there is obviously a great problem. I suggest it might he helpful if they got their acts together, we might say. Let them look at their respective acts and see if there is something that can be done. In that sense, and as I seem to have driven the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development out of the chamber completely, I will rest my case.

Before proceeding further, it is absolutely essential that I pay tribute to my predecessor, Senator Jack Marshall. There is tremendous respect for Mr. Marshall in my constituency. I share that respect. I have held him in high esteem for some time. In fact the esteem in which he is held by his former constituents was probably one of the few positive notes I found while on the campaign trail. I have committed myself to my constituents, and now commit myself to use Senator Marshall as a model of representation. He did a magnificent job of bringing his constituents' problems to the attention of this House.
I am here today to bring the message the people of Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe are sending to Ottawa by electing me to be their representative. They have spoken very clearly the feeling of many Newfoundlanders, namely, that the provincial Tory government and the federal Liberal government have not responded to their real needs.
We witnessed the situation in Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe during the course of the campaign of Liberal and Tory candidates and parachute helpers from other parts of Canada trying to justify the policies of their parties and the effects they have upon Newfoundland. This could not be done without some ridiculous posturing on their part.
The policies of both parties have, over the past few years, amounted to a serious attack on the fundamental foundations of the province of Newfoundland, the economy of that province, and my constituency in particular which, if it does not have the highest, has one of the highest rates of unemployment in this country.
In recent months the government has announced cutbacks in a number of programs essential to the operation of several industries in Newfoundland, the fishing industry in particular. Later it has relented or taken the sting out of its initial remarks. It is like saying to Newfoundland, "We know you are down, we have decided to kick you twice, but instead we will only kick you once." It is ridiculous to expect Newfoundlanders gratefully to accept this kind of relenting.
The message from Newfoundland in that constituency is that they are fed up with this kind of politics. The message goes further. The personal message I received from many constituents while on the campaign trail is that they cannot expect any different or any better from the two old line parties. The Liberals have shown by their record the priority they place on Newfoundland.
Let us look at what has happened in the last few months. The cutbacks in unemployment insurance are probably the most serious undermining of the economy on the west coast of Newfoundland in recent history. In the fishing industry, it will mean a loss of $18 million to the economy of Newfoundland. Overall, it will mean a loss of approximately $35 million, the lowest figure we have been able to obtain. It is horrendous to take that much out of the economy of a province that is now at rock bottom.
An official from a government department in Newfoundland, who will remain unnamed, said that these cutbacks will

national marketing board which would help not only Newfoundland fishermen but fishermen in all parts of Atlantic Canada and do for fishermen what the Wheat Board has done for farmers in the west. At the same time we recognize there is a distinct need for a short-term stimulus to the economy. This does not seem to be part of the policy policy of the other parties. There are many approaches which could be taken at this moment, for example, labour-intensive public works programs such as the upgrading of the railway and the development of harbours in Corner Brook and Stephenville. Small harbours could be upgraded or constructed throughout the province. These things could be done now; and they would provide an immediate stimulus, but long-term benefits to the economy would follow.
That is the message my constituents sent to Ottawa in electing me. They do not approve of what has been happening. They do not endorse the restraint and cutback mentality we have been hearing about over the past few months.
We in Newfoundland want to be an integral part of Confederation, contributing to its development. We do not want to exist on handouts for the next ten or 20 years. We have hopes of becoming in the future, perhaps, one of the "have" provinces, instead of being one of the six or seven "have-not" provinces. We do not want continuing high unemployment; we want to make a greater contribution to the economy.
We want jobs. We do not want to continue to receive unemployment insurance, which at the moment is a bigger contributor to our economy than the fishery. We want productivity to increase, and we want our people to be employed.
EIow can people have any dignity or pride in themselves as individuals or as a community if they do not have productive work of which they can be proud? This is the kind of thing upon which no positive action has been forthcoming from Ottawa, and I think the people of my riding have delivered a message. The message is that this has to change, hopefully as of now.

First, I want to congratulate the mover and seconder of this motion. speechtext:
Yet there is no doubt that Canada is a troubled country, and it is too facile and mindless an explanation to say that it is all or even largely a matter of leadership, whether federal or provincial or whether in the private or public sectors. The roots of our problem go deeper and are to be found within ourselves as individual Canadians. The maturity with which we face up to that fact, particularly in this House and particularly in the various elective bodies in this country, will determine the rate of our country's progress and, indeed, whether we have a country at all.
Here in Ottawa today our first ministers are meeting to discuss constitutional questions. These meetings remind me- and here I come to the explanation of what I said a few moments ago-that it was 30 years ago this month that I arrived in Ottawa for the first time and, still a foreigner, reported from the galleries and also participated in the negotiations of the terms under which Newfoundland would become a Canadian province. This weekend as I read over some of the documents relating to the first ministers' conference, I was struck forcibly by the fact that little has changed in 30 years or, I suppose for that matter, in the past 111 years of Canadian history. We are still a country with a tenuous hold on nationhood, and regardless of how much government critics may argue, as they always do, that the throne speech is empty, it highlights the goals which paradoxically have both divided and bound us together for more than a century: economic equality and national unity.
Time will not permit an assessment of all the elements in this intriguing and challenging puzzle. Much has been said already about economic matters, and since we are approaching the thirtieth anniversary of Newfoundland's entry into confederation, I propose to confine myself to some brief and necessarily incomplete references to national unity.
When I came to Ottawa first in 1948 I was convinced that there was no such thing as Canadian unity. I was fresh from a bitter referendum campaign in which it was argued, complete with Union Jacks, that confederation was British union, which prompted the retort, "British union with French Canada". Clearly, monarchist arguments and warnings about having French rammed down our throats are nothing new to me.
In 1948 I watched the whole issue of power sharing debated, not just between Newfoundland and Canada but with all the provinces chiming in for fear Newfoundland might in some

way get a better deal. Today, 30 years later, as we heard in the speech which preceded mine, little has changed; little, that is, except myself. On March 31, 1949, I became a Canadian, against my will. Born a Newfoundlander, I had opposed the union of my small country with Canada. Thus, with my province's entry I was compelled to test the validity of my new, unwanted country's demands on my loyalty and affection. As a result I am now proud to be a Canadian, strongly committed to national unity, and I hope, with the indulgence of hon. members, that what I have learned may be of some value in the present difficult period.
Newfoundland's resistance to union for so long provides further proof that regionalism is and always has been the strongest influence on Canadian development. Canadians are caught in a constant struggle between their intense regional loyalties and concern for Canada as a whole. Where the basis of this struggle is economic, reflecting a desire for material advancement, the motivation is roughly similar in all regions including Quebec. But when the language dimension is added, the essential difference emerges between the aspirations of Quebec and those of the rest of Canada. Even this distinction is an oversimplification. What is involved is French Canadian, not just Quebec alienation. Therefore the challenge is twofold: to lessen regional disparities generally, and, simultaneously and with equal commitment, to pursue all reasonable measures to give French Canadians in all parts of the country a true sense of belonging.
It is naive to assume, as the NDP and some others tend to argue from time to time, that separatism will be swept away on a rising tide of economic growth, or indeed, that the other threats to national unity posed by the many other manifestations of regionalism across the country are amenable to economic solutions alone. The present issue of Quebec separatism is not a lone aberration thrust on us suddenly to disturb the otherwise smooth and predictable flow of national development.
When this crisis passes, as I am sure it will, there are bound to be others in other regions. This is the price of diversity, whatever its compensating benefits. It is part of the perplexing dichotomy of Canada, and particularly of Canadian federalism. Each new wave of discontent prompts separatist rumblings, or at least a call for the drastic overhaul of structural arrangements. Witness, for example, as we all have, the constant references to western alienation and maritime disillusionment.
Canadians display an obvious ambivalence when, although taking a justifiable pride in their accomplishments, they often see these as having come about despite confederation, rather than because of it. Furthermore, their attitude is common to both weak and strong regions. For example, weakness brings claims that confederation perpetuates disparities. Strength breeds the confidence which reduces reliance on the centre. Yet, most of the time most Canadians, including the majority of Francophones, display a keen sense of nationhood and an
October 30, 1978

implicit awareness of the need to maintain the proper equilibrium between national and regional interests through the constant renewal of their commitment to the basic idea of Canada. It is that equilibrium, rather than many of its specific elements that change from time to time, which sustain the precarious balance that is at issue today.
The genius of confederation, I have come to discover, has been its acceptance of the respectability of compromise. Our federalism has been able to accommodate a remarkably wide range of often changing, disparate economic circumstances and interests, while maintaining the rough comparability of essential services required for national cohesion. This ability to employ creative pragmatism must be weighed now against the likely effectiveness of various current proposals for constitutional and structural changes. Central to most of these, as it always has been, and as we are hearing today in the Conference Centre, is the issue of power sharing between the federal government and the provinces. Also, there is a need for clarity on how much diversity in regional standards and practices Canadian federalism can tolerate before it becomes irretrievably fragmented. Both our history and present circumstances make it easy to understand why provincial leaders in both good and bad financial circumstances want more freedom to handle their own affairs.
Two gentlemen in the House right now, for whom I have the greatest respect, are former premiers of Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan. They will understand what I am talking about. While there is some logic in bringing decision making closer to those affected, this will not of itself remove the basic causes of our most intractable difficulties. It is my sincere conviction that belief that it will is one of the most serious weaknesses in the present Tory case, and indeed in others. The main sources of regional disparity lie elsewhere, and a more localized approach, as practical as it may be superficial, could produce fragmented, contradictory provincial policies. Changes which sharpen regional differences run the risk of diminishing our sense of nationhood still further.
Despite these real concerns, we must be prepared to embrace demonstrably beneficial new approaches, for Canadians and their leaders must feel they have the means to achieve their objectives. This is especially true for language rights and those economic and social opportunities to develop a sense of place and identity which we all desire so strongly, however difficult it is to undertake the task of articulating them with clarity and precision and without generating unfortunate misunderstanding.
The language problem has always been at the centre of the national unity issue. We ought to recognize that and state it factually, baldly and plainly. Even if the many economically motivated demands of regionalism can be met, through a combination of structural changes and what I have called creative pragmatism, millions of Francophones would still feel deprived in the language and cultural sense. Indeed, contrary to the views of hon. members opposite who lay the blame for current unrest at the feet of economic disparity, it has been greater economic security which has brought an upsurge of
The Address-Mr. Jamieson
interest in culturally centred objectives and the desire to identify more closely with origins or roots. Thus, although Francophone federalists and separatists disagree profoundly on means, all are seeking, in their own ways, self-fulfilment in the context of their own language and culture. The same aspirations are stirring noticeably in other parts of Canada, including my own where there has been a veritable renaissance in terms of the awareness of our people for their culture, folk music, tales, history and heritage.
Having rejected the fortress mentality of separatism, federalists must seek these goals within the broader, more diverse Canadian society which is increasingly receptive to accommodation, but still unclear and sometimes frustrated about what needs to be done.
Greater national unity can be achieved through actions in two broad categories. There are more facets to these categories, but I believe these can be stated objectively as being the two routes which can be followed: those flowing from laws and policies, and those reflecting a more understanding and responsive public attitude. Although the two are often mutually reinforcing, the principal opportunities for rapid, decisive movement lie in government action. I am referring to government in the plural. If we are logical in our assessment, we will recognize that much has been accomplished already.
But, the better climate responsible for these moves has been matched by the simultaneous emergence of increased tensions and the election of a separatist government in Quebec. I suggest this paradox is not coincidental, nor does the explanation lie in any faulty implementation of measures such as the Official Languages Act. Undoubtedly there were mistakes. There had to be with such a far reaching policy. They were inescapable. But the heightened reaction which we have witnessed over recent years, and which is so evident today, was the inevitable result of bringing long simmering, highly emotional grievances on both sides into sharper focus. Canadians, including those in my own province, have been obliged to confront a very fundamental issue, and many have been uncomfortable with the assignment. Latent prejudices and concerns were aroused, and fundamental differences were revealed between Anglophones and Francophones in their perception of the objectives of the act, and more broadly, of just what is needed to give Francophones a genuine and permanent sense of belonging.
I want to say something here that I think needs to be said, and needs to be said perhaps by an Anglophone and by one who is a relative newcomer to the Canadian federation. It is too easy to interpret many negative responses as a reflection of Anglophone bigotry and a stubborn determination to resist having French rammed down their throats. Of course, some of this exists, but there are understandable reasons for many Anglophone attitudes and misconceptions. For example, the Anglophone assumption is widespread, certainly in all parts of the country I have visited, and with the many thousands with whom I have spoken over the years, that most French Canadi-

October 30, 1978
The Address-Mr. Jamieson
ans are already bilingual and, as the saying goes, could speak French if they wished. Anything designed to expand the French language and its usage is not seen as a necessity but as an encroachment, or at best, an unnecessary complication.
Yet, Mr. Speaker, we who are here at the centre of the national government know, or we should know, that most Francophones, particularly in Quebec, speak only French and would have as much difficulty acquiring the second language as do most Anglophones. This, of course, is a basic concern of both language groups. Each fears the growth of bilingualism because of a generally realistic, and I emphasize this "generally realistic", awareness that second language competence is unattainable for most of them and will prove difficult even for their children.
These practical problems may be solvable over time through changes in the educational process but, even then, however, neither Anglophones nor Francophones are likely to want basic changes in the nature of their distinctive societies, their cultures and their lifestyles. This inescapable fact brings us to the heart of the dilemma, something upon which I am sure hon. members have spent many hours trying to figure out, that is, what the central or heart of the problem is-why this country, that I joined so reluctantly and have come to admire so much and want to see together, is being torn in this fashion today.
The inescapable fact is that reasonable people can subscribe to the proposition that there should be no barriers to opportunity in a united Canada. Unrestricted mobility in search of advancement is one of the long recognized advantages of Canadian citizenship. We are, in fact, as the records show, among the most mobile people in the world. But this principle of unlimited access, and this is a key point, runs squarely up against many of our regional characteristics and the desire and necessity to keep two linguistic communities, two distinctive cultures, alive and flourishing within the framework of two official languages.
In this context, therefore, the wish, as we hear it, to keep Quebec for Quebeckers and, inferentially, because the inference is clear, the rest of Canada for English-speaking Canadians, has an attraction for some in both camps because of its apparent simplicity. It is, however, dangerously superficial because it ignores the substantial French and English-speaking minorities whose problems would be seriously aggravated by such an arrangement. It tends also to provide a territorial basis for the two nations concept, incompatible with true federalism.
These then are some of the reasons, I suggest, why the Official Languages Act has been less than universally welcomed by both Anglophones and Francophones.
Francophones have the support of reasonable people for two entirely defensible propositions: Francophones should have full and equal access to employment opportunities in Englishspeaking Canada on the basis of merit; and, where their numbers warrant, they should be provided with services, including education of their families, in the French language. There is not, we all know, universal acceptance of these principles, of course, but Canadians of good will can see both the logic and justice, as well as the necessity for such meas-

ures. But, Mr. Speaker, and again perhaps this is not spoken often enough, and certainly not often enough in this House by those of us who have some responsibilities for leadership, it is equally logical, just, and necessary that Anglophones be aware and have the confidence that within the generally Frenchspeaking community, and particularly in Quebec, these same principles must apply in reverse: that, subject only to competence, Anglophones have equal access with Francophones to all employment and other opportunities; and that services, including education, be available under reasonable circumstances in the English language.
Here, of course, the difference between separatists and federalists emerges quite distinctly. Federalists, generally, accept these and similar principles. Separatists, while sometimes uttering confusing qualifications, clearly do not. But Anglophones are aware-I am aware as other Anglophones are aware, and this too is important-that even some federalist Francophones have expressed sympathy for the objectives of Bill 101, for example, even though disagreeing honestly and strongly with the methods it calls for. Anglophones are, therefore, concerned that their commitment to a free and open Canadian society may not be reciprocated by Francophones because the Francophones need to protect language, culture and identity will cause them, wherever and whenever possible, to wall in their community while resenting and resisting comparable moves by the English-speaking community.
This tendency to insulate is basic to the separatist approach. Federalists on the other hand, say simply, and I say it with them, "Let Quebec be primarily a French-speaking province just as, for example, Ontario or Newfoundland, for that matter, are English-speaking. But, let all the provinces recognize certain rights for their linguistic minorities." Quebec's Bills 22 and 101 go beyond this reasonable proposition and make matters more difficult and controversial by defining French as the sole official language rather than the working or principal language.
It is ironic, I should note parenthetically, that more widespread bilingualism is at best a mixed blessing to those Francophones who take this defensive approach to their goal of protection. English-speaking Canadians, however, must recognize and appreciate their right and determination, of which I have become very aware, to remain a distinct grouping, with their rich heritage and culture intact and assured for the future. The alternative is to accept the inevitable breakup of Canada, not merely through the separation of Quebec, but through the mounting discontent and alienation of the large number of Francophones who live in other parts of Canada for whom Quebec's separation offers no solution whatever.
The potential for misunderstanding, resentment and conflict is most acute where the two linguistic and cultural groups come in frequent and close contact; where the English or French-speaking minority is of very considerable proportions. In such areas and regions it is very much a matter of the two linguistic groups living together, and the utmost in reasonableness and understanding is called for in the search for a fair and permanent accommodation. Such understanding, I suggest to
October 30, 1978

you, cannot ignore the historic English language domination of most key elements of Canadian society, even in Quebec. The intangible effects of this traditional situation are legion, and are responsible for many of today's instinctive and negative reactions on both sides.
The frustrations and, hence, resentments caused by these developments must be recognized and understood. Such reactions are particularly acute in bilingual areas where job security and advancement are seen as being threatened, but everywhere in Canada there is an underlying concern that future economic and other opportunities will be denied those who are not bilingual. It is true, of course, as many bilingual Francophones-and I am sure some of my colleagues here would agree-are quick to point out, that they had to make the effort. But whatever the errors of history, these imperatives, in addition to providing the necessity also provided the opportunity, not only in bilingual communities but in a continent of over 200 million where English predominates. And, of course, although I have stated these concerns from the perspective of Anglophone Canadians, they are no less real for millions of unilingual Francophones.
Clearly, for practical, as well as less defensible reasons, educational systems across Canada have been and generally remain woefully deficient in their ability to teach the second language effectively. We now know also that language training for adults, as sponsored by the Government of Canada and others, cannot, in many cases, produce the desired results even for students whose motivation is strong.
When these practical considerations are linked with the less tangible, but no less real, concerns of Francophones for the preservation of their culture and heritage, the full dimension of the national unity problem is very obvious. In the minds of confirmed separatists many of these goals are mutually exclusive. The task of federalists, members of this House and all who are concerned about a united Canada, is to prove that they are not.
A key tool in this task is education. It has been noted repeatedly, but not always believed by Anglophones, that even today, after the introduction of Bill 101, Quebec still provides more by way of educational guarantees to its English-speaking minority than is provided for French language equivalents in other provinces. Yet, this is the case, and the faster corrective measures are taken, by way of constitutional guarantees and the implementation of new realistic approaches, the faster one of the main and most legitimate sources of Francophone grievance will be removed.
Education, and the greater comprehension and understanding it produces-

speechtext:
I am very grateful to the House, Mr. Speaker, and I assure hon. members that I will not impose on their time unnecessarily.
A key tool to this task is education, and the greater comprehension and understanding it produces is the only alternative to the seige mentality, to the "two nations" concept, and to separatism itself. Those who argue for these alternatives fail to realize in most cases that they would produce, not just one watertight compartment, but two, and this situation might very well lead to still more as other regions, although all in English-speaking Canada, sought to erect their own barriers to protect characteristics or advantages they consider important.
I am seeing signs of that already in my own part of the country. I believe it to be very, very negative in terms of national unity. I hope that I will have the opportunity to persuade people in my province, for example, that this seige mentality, this idea that it is a "we and they" situation is counter to the very thing for which we fought such a bitter referendum 30 years ago.
Canadian federalism-and I know now after 30 years perhaps better than most because of this unique background that I happen to have, which is not of my own doing-is either totally open or eventually it is nothing. The diversity various regions prize can only be assured through a climate of openness and through policies and approaches that encourage and nourish regional attitudes, including language rights, while at the same time exposing them to the test of relevancy and value.
While putting great emphasis on education, we must, of course, continue to take other steps toward greater national unity. Some of considerable importance have their roots in constitutional reform, a subject that will be much discussed in coming months. It is clear from all of the dramatic developments in Canada in recent years that the time for leisurely, piecemeal dialogue on national unity is over. The election of a separatist government in Quebec is not the only reason for the new urgency; in some respects it is not even the most important. Its greatest significance is the much sharper focus it has given to an historic, ever present problem. It would be a major mistake, however, to assume that the defeat of the Parti Quebecois will end the problem. The task of reconciliation and reform pre-dates the Parti Quebecois victory and will remain to be completed after the Parti Quebecois is gone.
Those who maintain that defeating the separatists can be left solely to the people of Quebec are only right in the narrow sense that it is Quebeckers who will vote in the referendum, and the provincial election when it comes. But, while these actions may defeat Quebec separatism as a referendum issue, they will not of themselves save Canada. There is a real danger that the ousting of the Parti Quebecois government will be seen by many Canadians-indeed, it is already being perceived by many Canadians-as the definitive judgment on separatism.
But, even on the narrower issue, all Canadians have an obvious stake in the referendum. That stake is not just the future of Quebec, but the future of Canada. Therefore, in addition to stating unequivocally what is unacceptable to

October 30,1978
The Address-Mr. Jamieson
Canada in the Parti Quebecois referendum proposals, it is essential that the Quebeckers be told by their federal government what the federalist options are, and shown how their legitimate aspirations can be achieved best within the Canadian framework. It is unthinkable that the rest of Canada should stand aloof from such a momentous struggle, and those Quebecers, including some federalists, who see this issue as their concern alone, may be well-meaning, but they are wrong.
The Parliament and Government of Canada represent and speak for all Canadians, including Quebeckers, on national issues and in areas of federal responsibility. Nothing fits these criteria more than the threatened dismemberment of the country. There should be no doubts; separatism is the enemy of all Canadians, and all Canadians must oppose it vigorously.
But while separatism is the most urgent and direct threat to unity, it is not the only one. The comprehensive renewal process should not be distorted or compacted into an effort that is directed primarily at the separatist crisis. Other groups and other regions also have problems and doubts. The larger task is to embrace all of these, to find means whereby we can not only lessen grievances but make the entire federal system more responsive and a better instrument for identifying and carrying out the national will.
And there is a national will, I have discovered, a strong Canadian sense of nationhood. It is something more than the distillation of ten provincial government views, the common denominator achieved through the melding of ten often disparate viewpoints, worked and reworked until a consensus appears. Given the complexity of our times, such exercises in co-operation are important, even though not accorded great weight by Canada's founders, nor its leaders during our first half century. The number of federal-provincial or dominion-provincial conferences were few and far between for the first 50 or 60 years of our history.
These founders wisely created a national government, a Government and Parliament of Canada, to represent and speak for all Canadians, the citizens of one nation. Today, just as it is the responsibility of that government and parliament to fight separatism and provide a counterweight to excessive regionalism, it must also articulate national goals, not merely in economic and materials terms, but in ways that will define more clearly-and I have reason to know this through my present responsibilities-to ourselves and to the world what Canada is and for what it stands. Only through such widely shared understanding, Mr. Speaker, can we strengthen the national will still further and share a common pride in the whole of Canada, while fostering and drawing strength and satisfaction from the positive elements of our remarkable diversity.
In this context, while the provinces may be regarded as the bricks of confederation, the Government and Parliament of Canada provide the mortar that binds them into a solid enduring structure. Thus, while the whole is the sum of its parts-and this we forget at our peril-it also has a shape and

form of its own. To prevent erosion, formal mechanisms are essential; but these alone will not ensure a strong Canada. Canadians cannot rely on them entirely but must also possess the will to continue living together and to continue saying with pride, "I am a Canadian".
We in Newfoundland have never been at all ashamed of wearing our hearts on our sleeves, perhaps because of the Gaelic background of most of us. In any event, one of those difficult adjustments I had to make as a Canadian was to what I used to describe as "good grey Canadianism"-the kind of feeling that it was somehow improper, or at least modestly incorrect, to express pride in our country, to talk out loud about what this nation means to us. I went through a period when I assumed a part of that greyness, but now I am convinced most sincerely that we have to shrug off what one might describe as a kind of uneasiness or discomfort with the rhetoric of nationhood and say what we think of this country.
Against that background let me conclude by saying that I began with a declaration of personal pride in Canada and of my commitment to work for national unity. Having experienced one identity crisis in my life, I have no wish to contemplate another, because, believe me, it was a traumatic experience. Canada, all of it, is now my home, and no man could ask for better. Through the tremendous advantages that have been given to me by Canada, through these opportunities that have been given to me as a member of parliament and as someone who speaks for Canada to the world, I have come to realize that a variety of circumstances, not all of our making, not always something for which we can take any credit, just God's natural goodness, have brought together on our half of the North American continent a unique combination of the ingredients that give us, as Canadians, a better way of life- not better by comparison with other people in other lands, although most are envious of our good fortune, but better in the sense that these scores of elements, from climate to natural wealth, from majestic scenery and vast open spaces to cleaner, more well-ordered cities, and comfortable, relaxed small towns and villages, from our proud beginnings and our native peoples to our present exciting mixture of races and cultures-all of these and so many more have shaped and responded to our special aspirations as a unique people, Canadians, and have contrived, often without our help, to add joy to our lives, rewards for our labours, and boundless hope for our individual and common futures.
I am grateful to the House for giving me this extra time, but sometime in the future, on the thirtieth anniversary of some other provinces' entry, if there are more, or when people are looking over it, I want to have on record what I thought about this country after 30 years as a Canadian.
Truly I believe we are the most fortunate country on earth. I have no doubt we will keep it that way.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to begin by offering my congratulations to the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) for the passion he
October 30, 1978

put into his remarks, a passion which I am sure stems from the fact that he recognizes the many serious problems facing this country are a direct result of the actions of the government of which he is a member. I want to say that a subject about which I feel equally passionate is scientific research. I have spoken about this a number of times in this chamber, but I am sorry to say that on all of those occasions the suggestions I have put forward have fallen on deaf ears on the government side.
To try to explain the situation a little more clearly or simply, I have to revert to a segment of my life which happened long ago. You may not be aware, Mr. Speaker, that one of the things I retired from to come to this place was farming. I am a retired farmer, so in talking about research in Canada I want to make reference to the farm where I used to live.
As you know, there are a number of animals and birds on farms-horses, cattle, sheep-such as those on the other side of this House. The bird I wanted to deal with particularly is the goose. Everyone knows that the goose lays eggs and that these are a useful commodity. Everybody knows, too, that a goose egg is the symbol for something not very valuable, or perhaps that even represents failure. That is only the case if it is a normal goose egg, of course, but if it happens to be a golden egg, that changes the picture.
I want to spend some time talking about the golden egg. The farmers to whom I am referring, namely, the people of Canada, are fortunate because the goose they own happens to lay golden eggs. That goose is the medical and scientific research community of this country.
We know that in order for a goose to produce, it must have certain things. It requires nourishment-by way of corn, perhaps; it requires shelter-a place to build its nest where it can lay the golden eggs; and it requires some water and some general care. If care is given to the goose it will produce golden eggs every day, every week, every month, and perhaps every year.
That is not to say that a goose is the only animal or bird on a farm. We recognize that there are other animals that need to be fed some of the same corn that the goose needs. It is a question of deciding in times of restraint which should be fed the most or the least.
As I recollect, if there were pet cats or dogs they were generally considered by the farmer to be non-productive and perhaps were even sacrificed during times of restraint or lack of food. Unfortunately, the government we have, has chosen to starve the goose which lays the golden egg, and has chosen to feed greater and greater shares to the pet cats and dogs.
Canada, in common with other developed nations, largely depends on science and technology to maintain and develop its standard of living. Unlike governments in other industrialized countries, the Government of Canada has for the last ten years shown a total lack of concern for the need to develop an adequate fund of scientific and technical knowledge or scientifically and technically educated people. In essence, the Gov-
The Address-Mr. Yewchuk
ernment of Canada has been satisfied to base our standard of living on depleting natural resources and on using the scientific, and technical knowledge and efforts of other countries.
When the government has spent money, it is clear the spending has not been done in anything that resembles an optimum fashion. Rather than asserting strong leadership by committing itself to support research and development, rather than striving to create a science and technology infrastructure that could provide the critical underpinning for industrial and socioeconomic programs, the government has discouraged innovation. It has discouraged hard work; it has discouraged productivity. Instead, the government has chosen to spend the taxpayers' money on creating a huge unwieldy and largely inefficient bureaucracy. Surely this direction is not the road to economic progress.
Few Canadians would pretend that it is easy to establish a comprehensive, scientific and industrial strategy. But unlike those who sit on the other side of the House, we in the Progressive Conservative party will not be dissuaded by issues bearing on ease of accomplishment. We reject categorically any short-term politically-expedient answers to our problems stemming from deindustrialization and scientific-technological insufficiency. We do this in the certain belief that Canada needs to grow and create new wealth. In other words, we need to have new golden eggs, to put it in simple language for the other side, for the benefit of all Canadians in every province. We do this because we recognize that the principle element of any national growth strategy is already visible. Canada, like all other successful western industrialized countries, must emphasize research and development and high technology if it is to compete successfully in the world.
The Progressive Conservative party believes the future of Canada is at least as important as the present. We must look to the future by working diligently to solve the many problems that exist today. The cornerstones of Canada's thrust toward a healthy science base should be similar to those of any other high priority national effort. A science strategy, like an industrial strategy or cultural strategy, will need to be based on existing strengths and needs of our country, on coherence and relevance, and on co-operation between the federal and provincial governments, industry, business, universities, and the lay community.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, a scientific industrial strategy must be based on continuity and stability since progress in science is utterly dependent on the continuing infusion of ambitious, productive and creative new talent. So to state it again in simple terminology, the golden goose indeed does have the capability of reproducing, or at least to regenerate some of its lost parts. In other words, if one plucks a feather, the goose can grow a new one. So it is not too late to correct the wrongs of government shortsightedness.
For the benefit of those Liberal members who for so long neglected science and technology, I would like to point out that Canadians, in spite of the government's negligence, have demonstrated excellence in both basic and applied research in many fields and disciplines. In the area with which I am most
606

October 30, 1978
The Address-Mr. Yewchuk
familiar, biomedical research, the list of Canadian research accomplishments is both long and impressive. This is the list of golden eggs that I want to put on the record. For example, Dr. Sourkes of Montreal and Dr. McGeer of Vancouver jointly elucidated the cause of Parkinson's disease, a condition which causes uncontrollable shakiness in certain individuals; Dr. Robinson of Vancouver has developed a method for controlling rheumatoid diseases; Dr. Noble, also of Vancouver, has discovered an important group of anti-cancer drugs; Dr. Nickerson, also of Vancouver, has developed drugs used in the treatment of high blood pressure.
Dr. Merrimam of Saskatoon has demonstrated the relationship between grain dust and chest disease and has also pioneered work on the role of exercise in coronary heart disease; Dr. Kirkaldy-Willis' work in Saskatoon has improved methods of managing low back pain; Dr. Harold Johns, formerly of Saskatoon and now working at the Ontario Cancer Institute in Toronto, discovered and developed a Cobalt 60 unit for radiation treatment of cancer; Drs. Gold and Freedman of Montreal developed an extremely important diagnostic test for bowel cancer; Drs. Horlick and Sodhi of Saskatoon-there are a lot of good scientists in Saskatoon, some good politicians, and some bad ones too-clarified the role of high fat levels in atheroschlerosis and their control with drugs; Dr. Chang of Toronto developed a purification cartridge for portable artificial kidney machines; Dr. Bruce, also of Toronto, developed the rationale for combination cancer therapy.
This listing of major accomplishments by Canadian biomedical researchers is by no means all-inclusive. It does, nonetheless, clearly indicate that in addition to the highly publicized achievements of people like Wilder Penfield, Hans Selye. J. B. Collip, D. H. Copp, Fredrick Banting and Charles Best, this country has many other scientists of first-class international standing.
Canada does not lack scientific talent; rather, it lacks a science policy which would allow researchers to contribute to improving the health and well-being of Canada and the economy of the nation. The government that we are faced with today in this chamber deals with health research as if it were an expensive charitable budgetary outflow. The fact is that health research expenditures by the federal government constitute less than 0.2 per cent of the total budget, and less than 1 per cent of the Department of National Health and Welfare budget. Furthermore, there is now ample documentation that funds spent on health research are a prudent investment for reducing health care costs in the future. They are not a charitable expense without any tangible fiscal benefits.
You may be asking, Mr. Speaker, what that means, and perhaps even members on the other side might be curious about how much one of these golden eggs is worth. It might even be thought "Who cares about golden eggs? They be worth nothing." However, I can assure hon. members that the value of gold is very high these days, and I would like to give an indication of what these golden eggs are worth. For example, Dr. Bob Hickie of the University of Saskatchewan has recently completed a study which shows that for every dollar

invested in health research, the minimum return within ten years by way of permanently reduced health care costs is at least $20.
The total research cost for developing poliomyelitis vaccine was $41 million. The estimated saving to Canada since that time has been about $200 million per year since 1955. Just consider that saving, for a small investment. The saving due to this discovery alone more than pays for all the health research done in Canada since that year.
Measles immunization has resulted in a saving to Canadians of at least $10 million per year. Treatment of hemophilia saves Canadians $20 million per year in hospitalization costs alone, not to mention the suffering of patients which has been reduced. Basic research into the cause of blindness in premature babies cost $34,000. The annual saving due to the averted blindness is $24,000 for every dollar spent on research.
The discovery of the antibiotic streptomycin used for treatment of tuberculosis has saved Canadians $30 million per year since 1952. Penicillin continues to save more lives each year than were lost during the entire Second World War. Just consider that, for a government which looks on research as a charitable outflow. If typhoid fever were treated today by 1935 standards, the patient would have to be hospitalized for about 50 days at a cost of about $8,500; now the costs include a prescription for chloramphenical at about $5, and one or two days of fever.
The basic research by Canadian scientists into the defect associated with Parkinsonism and its treatment with L-DOPA saves Canadians at least $120 million per year. A diagnostic test for cancer of the bowel, also developed by Canadian scientists, saves Canadian taxpayers about $60 million per year. The total cost of discovering insulin by Drs. Banting and Best was less than $30,000; though not yet documented, the total monetary saving to Canadians since the discovery in 1921 would be staggering.
The lives and livelihood that have been spared by cures and treatments resulting from basic and applied biomedical research during the last 40 years have been estimated by Creditel of Canada Limited to save Canadians $1.7 billion this year. This saving represents nearly 10 per cent of the total budget of the Department of National Health and Welfare.
We believe that the government's expenditures are in general excessively high, and in some areas outright wasteful. As I mentioned, this government can be compared with the farmer who feeds too many cats and other family pets which are not productive. We believe also, however, that spending in the area of research and development should be regarded as a needed investment, not as a loss of federal dollars. It is not a loss or simple expenditure. Federal investment in this area must increase, not decrease, because it is clear that scientific innovation could play an essential role in achieving many of Canada's economic objectives, a strong manufacturing sector with consequent growth of employment opportunities, industrial effectiveness leading to greater price stability and a stronger value
October 30, 1978

for our dollar, positive international trade balance in high-technology manufactured products, good quality cost-effective health care, and a strong, confident, and visionary scientific community.
The government's proposals to cut back further on investment in research and development and the closely related area of post-secondary education are ludicrous. They are tantamount not only to starving the golden goose, but to plucking its feathers and cutting off some of its limbs.
It is truly a quixotic government policy that, on June 1 of this year, proposes to stimulate scientific and technological growth in this country and then, just a few months later, it reneges on the same promises by cutting back on investment.
The proposed cutback in science and technology activities will adversely affect the research performance of most government departments and all Canadian universities. The Department of Agriculture would lose $8.5 million from its science budget; the Department of Environment, $11.7 million; the Department of Fisheries, $11.1 million; and the Department of National Health and Welfare, $10.3 million. The three extramural research granting councils, already desperately short of funds to support scientists and provide equipment and support staff, would lose a total of $3.1 million.
The ramifications of the proposed cut of $0.5 million in the budget of the Medical Research Council and $2 million in the National Health Research and Development program will be much more extensive than simply its effect on the investigators themselves.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) continue to pluck the feathers off the golden goose. Perhaps they will be used for a pillow to make the Prime Minister more comfortable, the pillow being the PMO. There have been no cutbacks in the Prime Minister's office, only in research and other areas. The effect on health care in Canada of this loss of research potential and trained personnel will be particularly severe and will affect the formation and development of cost-effective health care policies. In addition, this loss will affect the training of physicians, other health professionals, research scientists, and will directly affect patient care, as trained personnel leave Canada for other countries which recognize and support scientific research.
These losses will be irreparable. Obviously if you cut the head off the golden goose there will be no more golden eggs. It will be impossible to replace trained staff, and there will be a cessation of valuable research programs which have taken many years to develop. These programs will not be able to be started again on short notice when the fiscal climate becomes more favourable, as it will when a Conservative government takes over, as it takes many years to recruit skilled scientists and to train new staff. There is no doubt that there will be a reluctance among skilled scientists to work in a country which has so clearly shown its lack of interest in and continued commitment to research.
The Address-Mr. Yewchuk
One example of a health research program which will be discontinued if these proposed cuts are implemented will serve to illustrate the lack of vision from which this government suffers.
In the Department of Pediatrics at the University of Manitoba, Dr. Judith Sayed, one of the very few pediatric nutrionists in Canada, and a National Health Scholar, is investigating the nutrition and nutrition-based diseases in Indian and Inuit children in Manitoba and the Northwest Territories. A number of previously unsuspected problems have already been found. Rickets, a vitamin deficiency disease, thought to have been abolished in Canada, still exists among children in remote Indian communities. Intolerance to milk due to deficiencies in gastrointestinal motility, is very common among older Indian and Inuit children and may contribute to diarrheal illness. The high incidence of infectious diseases among Indian infants is, in large part, due to a mistaken preference for bottle over breast feeding. As a result of these findings, remedies are already under way to improve the health of native children.
The Medical Research Council is the main source for biomedical research funding in Canada. That body provides most of the corn to feed the golden goose. It provides approximately 50 per cent of the total $130 million currently spent on health research. Under the current administration the growth of the MRC budget, particularly since 1971, has been painfully inadequate. The measure of corn for the goose has been smaller and smaller. The increases during the past eight years have not even kept pace with the cost of living increase, let alone the inflation costs of scientific equipment, materials and reagents which have been increasing by at least 15 per cent per year and at present exceed 20 per cent taking into account the 85 cent Canadian dollar.
In terms of the total budget of the Department of National Health and Welfare, the MRC budget has fallen from 1.33 per cent in 1971-72 to 1.30 per cent in 1972-73, to 1.14 per cent in 1973-74, to 0.87 per cent in 1974-75. Currently, the MRC receives approximately 0.6 per cent of the total budget of Health and Welfare. The ratio has gone down by about two thirds.
On June 1 the government announced it was going to devote 1.5 per cent of its gross domestic product to research funding. It proposed regional "centres of excellence", innovation centres, and changes in government procurement policy to stimulate Canadian research and development. All these things were swept aside only eight weeks later.
That is why there needs to be a change in government. The Prime Minister has decided to eat the goose's corn. Indeed, he is poised to eat the goose itself.
The Conservative party stated on an opposition day not too long ago that we are committed to directing 2.5 per cent of the gross national product toward scientific research, a program to be implemented over five to seven years. We are talking about trebling or quadrupling the measure of corn for the golden
608

October 30, 1978
The Address-Mr. Richardson
goose. Such a measure will at least enable us to catch up with the level of funding practised in the United States and other industrialized western nations.
To sum up, the Liberal government is starving and dismembering the research community. The Prime Minister has not only reduced the amount of corn available to the golden goose, he has plucked its feathers and pulled off one leg for a meal; he is now holding it over the chopping block by the remaining leg. Why, one might ask, is he doing this since it is so obviously the wrong thing to do? Well, perhaps he does not care about the golden goose. Perhaps he just wants to eat the goose. We, as the party of the alternative government, propose to correct this disastrous policy and to restore the research community to a healthy status so that it can continue to carry out the research which is necessary if this country is to be a viable and competitive nation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for more than two years, since I resigned from the cabinet, I have been warning the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that he was leading Canada in the wrong direction, that his policies would do more to divide the nation than to unite it. The fundamental flaw in the policies of the Liberal government is that they emphasize our differences as Canadians instead of emphasizing all that unites us as Canadians.
I have had the opportunity to give this warning on many occasions-here in the House in the debate on the Speech from the Throne a year ago, before the Pepin-Robarts Task Force on Canadian Unity this January, and when I crossed the floor of the House in June of this year. Now that we have seen the results of the 15 by-elections on October 16, to see that the Canadian people are trying to tell the Prime Minister and the government that they are going in the wrong direction, that they are doing more to divide the country than to unite it, it is all I can do to resist saying, "1 told you so."
My warning has not been confined to the national unity issue. More than two years ago, when I was writing my letter of resignation to the Prime Minister, I said:
I do not believe the government has fully recognized and utilized for the common good the energies and creativity of Canadian entrepreneurs. The bureaucracy is still too big and government is still interfering too much in the working of the economy.
That was more than two years ago. Now, at last, in the Speech from the Throne the government is talking about, and I quote, "the private sector leading the way towards accelerated growth". The Speech from the Throne goes on to talk about "encouraging a more vigorous expansion of the private sector by reducing the governmet's share of the national wealth."
The words are beginning to sound right, Mr. Speaker. The government has finally learned to say the right thing even though it is not yet clear whether the government really understands its own words and, more particularly, whether it really believes its own words. Only the budget which has been promised for next month will show whether the government's new-found confidence in the private sector is anything more than empty rhetoric. Only the budget will reveal whether the government is capable of understanding how to restore inves-

tor confidence, both Canadian and international investor confidence; because that is the essential first step in revitalizing and strengthening the Canadian economy.
Today, as members of parliament, we find ourselves in an extraordinary situation. We have just read a Speech from the Throne which calls for national unity. It comes from the same government that gave us the constitutional amendment bill, Bill C-60, which is one of the most divisive pieces of legislation ever placed before parliament. For example, it calls for a double majority, a French and an English majority, on matters of linguistic significance in the new, proposed House of Federation. This proposed legislation also calls for two classes of Supreme Court judges. Certain judges will be able to make judgments in relation to the civil code and common law. Others will only be able to make judgments about the common law. Surely two classes of judges cannot be based on a one-nation concept?
Then we find the preamble to the constitution in this new legislation. The preamble spends more time trying to describe our differences as Canadians than in trying to encourage our unity. Legislation of this sort cannot possibly unite Canada. I do not think it is enough for the government to say it will revise the legislation, as promised in the Speech from the Throne. The government is so completely on the wrong track that it will be necessary, as I said in the special committee, to put Bill C-60 into the shredder and start over again with a new concept which could really help achieve a united Canada.
Fortunately for Canada, the democratic process is at work. There is widespread opposition to Bill C-60 and to the government's proposals for constitutional amendment. The premiers unanimously opposed the legislation at their meeting in Regina, and though I have not heard the whole of the proceedings at the conference today it appears they are saying the same things today as they did then. Also, the Senate is opposed to the proposals-and not just to protect itself, as some have wrongly suggested, but for much more fundamental reasons.
Wide sections of the media are opposed, and growing numbers of the public are opposed, so we have all this opposition to the constitutional amendment bill, and it is very clear that the democratic process is working. It has been made clear that the government's proposals for constitutional change are clearly not a reflection of the national will.
Despite this widespread and really overwhelming opposition, the Prime Minister gives ever indication of wanting to lock his vision of Canada into the constitution. He still wants to proceed with his vision of Canada. In the throne speech debate the Prime Minister spoke for more than an hour and a half, but one sentence revealed his thinking better than anything else he said in that long debate. When the Prime Minister was talking about the constitution giving protection to his concept of language equality, hon. members who were here on October 12 will recall that he said that it was not really vital to him whether the Supreme Court had nine judges or 11 judges. He said it was not really vital to him whether the House of the
October 30, 1978

Federation was directly elected or elected by the political parties.
The all-important sentence in his whole speech can be found at page 37 of Hansard for October 12, 1978. The Prime Minister said:
It is vital to me that it-
He was referring to the constitution: "that the constitution":
-does give protection to the kind of linguistic equality that this government has put into the statutes.
What does the Prime Minister mean by "give protection"? Clearly, he means that he wants to give protection from parliament. He wants to protect his legislation from any amendment by future parliament. He wants to place his legislation beyond the reach of parliament. Recently I read an article by a newspaper columnist who said that the Prime Minister is prepared to give up power and to give up authority. This columnist was right in this way: The Prime Minister is prepared to give up power and authority, but he is not prepared to give up his power and his authority. What he is prepared to do is give up the authority and the power of his successors to change what he has done.
The Prime Minister obviously does not believe in the supremacy of parliament: he believes in the supremacy of a written constitution.
As recently as this morning when he was opening the federal-provincial constitutional conference, the Prime Minister said, "We want a Canada in which we are all bound by one law," the law of the constitution. I do not believe that Canadians want to be bound by anything, and certainly not by a Trudeau-written constitution. I think members of parliament should be warned by the sentence I have read from the Prime Minister's speech and they should be ready to defend the supremacy of parliament over the supremacy of a written constitution.
I receive thousands of letters from Canadians on this subject, and the people of Canada do not want the supremacy of a Trudeau-written constitution to replace the supremacy of a democratically elected parliament.
The Speech from the Throne talks about good will and about flexibility on all sides. I believe the trouble is that the government wants flexibility from everyone but does not want to be flexible itself. One example of inflexibility over the years has been the Prime Minister has insisted on an amending procedure which gives a single province the power of veto.
I know that today there is some general talk about looking at other forms of amending procedure, but ever since 1968 the Prime Minister, in his letters to provincial premiers and in other ways, has never varied from the Victoria formula, which called for a perpetual veto for Ontario and a perpetual veto for Quebec. We do not have to draw pictures to explain that when we are dealing with linguistic matters a perpetual veto for Quebec has more significance than a veto for other provinces. We should be aware that there is no federal state in the world which gives to one of its constituent parts, that is, a province, a state or a canton, the same right to approve or disapprove amendments to the constitution that belong to the nation itself,
The Address-Mr. Richardson
and yet that is what the Prime Minister is proposing. He is proposing a single province veto.
I have made several proposals for amending procedures of the kinds used in other countries. I have proposed referenda and a two-thirds majority of an upper house. There are several possibilities. What they all have in common is that they would be a reflection of the national will. I think it is vital that we amend our constitution with a consensus of the people of Canada as a whole and not that we find ourselves placed under the veto of a single province.
The last thing I want to say regarding amendment of the constitution is something which has been mentioned by others, but it is so important that it requires emphasis and repetition. This government does not have a mandate to make fundamental constitutional changes. I remember the 1974 election, as other hon. members do, but there was no discussion of the constitution in those days. We talked about wage and price controls and about other matters. We discussed the constitution in earlier years, so we cannot say that it is just because of the Quebec election of November, 1976, that we are now discussing the constitution. We discussed the constitution before the 1972 election, but not before the 1974 election. If we check the records, I think we will find that there has been very little discussion of the constitution or constitutional amendment, so the government does not have a mandate, particularly in this fifth and dying year of the government, to expect the Canadian people to agree to see fundamental changes in the constitution. That is totally unthinkable.
In passing, it is perhaps worth making the point that we are talking about fundamental change. The Prime Minister likes to use the word "renewal". He talks about renewal of the federation, but I think we should all be aware and be warned that "renewal" is a buzz word. It is a catch word. It is intended to hide the truth. From now on, every time members of parliament and the public read the words "renewal of the federation," I ask them to read "fundamental change " in the federation. Then we will be closer to understanding what the Prime Minister is really trying to do.
Fortunately for Canada, there is an answer to Canadian unity. It is the answer we have always known, and we have lost it only for a little while. Once again it is being presented and articulated by a group of citizens who call themselves Canadians For One Canada. They have set out in clear and precise terms the principles on which they believe Canada can be built as a truly united nation. If the Speech from the Throne had been based upon these principles, today we would be on our way to becoming a truly united nation once again, to being one Canada, instead of being divided and confused by the government's false concepts of duality, diversity, and division.
Canadians For One Canada believe above all in a truly united Canada. These are their firmly held beliefs and principles as contained in their brochure. Their first belief is that Canada is a partnership of all Canadians and not just a partnership of two founding races.

October 30, 1978
The Address-Mr. Richardson
Second, they believe that it should be possible for all Canadians to be united by a common national language and, at the same time, to welcome and respect the French language as an important regional language.
Their third belief is that the serious problem of language difference does not exist in most of Canada, but is essentially a regional problem which can be solved regionally by Frenchspeaking and English-speaking Quebeckers becoming increasingly bilingual. Surely this is the common sense answer which provides Quebec with the best of both worlds and, at the same time, achieves a truly united Canada.
The fourth belief of Canadians For One Canada is that the attempt to entrench nation-wide French-English language equality in the constitution only extends the problem of language difference; it does not solve it. Also they believe that amendments to the Constitution of Canada must not be controlled by the veto of any single province, but must always be a reflection of the national will.
Finally, central to the whole concept is their firmly held conviction that Canada is one country and Canadians are one people. As soon as the beliefs and principles of one Canada are written into a future speech from the throne, Canada will be well on the way to becoming a united nation, a truly united nation, once again.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have said many times that as long as we can leave the difficult problem of language at the level of statutory law, I see no problem. I am referring to Bill 101 at the provincial level and the Official Languages Act at the federal level. Laws made by parliament or by the national assembly, as in the case of Bill 101, can be amended by future generations of Canadians and parliamentarians. I am opposed to taking the principles of the Official Languages Act and locking them into the Constitution of Canada under a rigid amending procedure which, for all practical purposes, prevents amendment. In other words, it is the locking up for the future to which I am really opposed. I do not think a law passed by the House, or by the Quebec National Assembly, is forever a law. It can be amended. Therefore, I see no problem with Bill 101. But one should read carefully what is in Bill C-60 because

it entrenches Bill 101. It is wrong to tie the hands of future generations of Canadians in that manner.
