speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before getting into the comments I wish to make this afternoon, I should like to refer to a couple of the suggestions made by the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson). His concept of Canada is certainly one which will never bring unity or harmony to the country. Where is the equality in having one national language and one regional language? Where is the equality in providing language guarantees to English-speaking Canadians in Quebec only in federal legislation and not entrenched in the constitution? How would language guarantees be provided to Anglophones in Quebec, especially with a government like the Parti Quebecois in power? That government wants to make Quebec a unilingual province.
At the federal level we have been working since 1969, when the Official Languages Act was proclaimed, to make the country officially bilingual. The hon. member was in cabinet for some eight years when that law was passed. I am sure he supported it. His suggestions and ideas would take us back to the 1960s before the Bilingualism and Biculturalism Commission held its hearings and came up with the principles of the Official Languages Act. It provides for services by the federal government in either official language where there is a significant minority.
If we accept the concept of the hon. member of a unilingual Canada, one official language, how does a French-speaking unilingual person from the province of Quebec travel to western or eastern Canada with the announcements on the aircraft, train or whatever, being in the English language only? The concepts espoused by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the premiers at the constitutional conference in Ottawa today indicate that they are working toward making this country united, whole and one.
I should like to congratulate the hon. member for York South (Mrs. Appolloni) and the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Savard) for their excellent speeches in opening this debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. The Speech from the Throne emphasized two things: the matter of the constitution, and the economy of our country. Today we see an outgrowth of that, the heads of government meeting at the Conference Centre in Ottawa to deal with the constitution. We look forward with great anticipation to the success of that conference.
In the matter of the economy, which is really very much on the mind of every member as we reassemble in this final session of this parliament, we see the initiatives which were announced in early August further amplified in the Speech from the Throne; the reduction in government expenditures during the next two fiscal years of $2.5 billion, a move toward seeing the Post Office made into a Crown corporation, a commitment by the government to provide incentives and stimulus to the private sector amounting to some $300 million
October 30, 1978

this coming year, and the re-ordering of our priorities for another $1 billion during this coming year.
It is significant that even though there have been dramatic and very difficult reductions in expenditures of $2.5 billion during this period of time, the government was still able to announce important changes to the kind of social programs we have in this country; aid and assistance for low wage earners, assistance to families with a large number of children, and assistance to our senior citizens, those who do not have other forms of income. We see that, even in the face of very severe cutbacks, our social programs will continue; for instance, the increase in the provision of the family allowance program where, although we will still be providing $20 per month per child, there will be provision for a cheque of $200 per child a year or refundable tax credit available to families earning less than $18,000 and graduating up from there. This will benefit some 2.4 million families, involving at least five million children. At the same time, the guaranteed income supplement will be increased by some $20 starting with the January cheque.
In face of the problems of inflation, an improvement as well was the reduction in excise tax on gasoline of some three cents a gallon, and a move by the government to try to hold down the increase in the crude oil price by $1 a barrel, an increase which would have otherwise gone into effect on January 1.
I must compliment the federal government on being able to equalize the price of crude oil right across the country, with minor variations for transportation costs, because in my constituency one of the very hot issues is the fact that we have such a wide variation, sometimes ten, 12 or 15 cents a gallon, in the retail price of gasoline. This is a responsibility of the provincial government in respect of which it has been reluctant to move to give some uniformity across the province, as the federal government has done in respect of crude oil, which is its responsibility. It seems to me that if the oil companies are unable to give us a more fair and equitable pricing mechanism, the province should move in an attempt to provide some equity in respect of retail gasoline prices, as the federal government has been able to do with crude oil prices.
We have to be careful when we listen to speeches on the motion in respect of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, such as those we hear from opposition benches, that we do not get caught up in all of this gloom and doom they send across the aisle to us, and across the country by way of television and radio.
If we look at many sectors of our economy today we will see some very positive signs. If you look at the merchandise trade figures which were released last Friday you will see that we are heading toward a $4 billion merchandise trade surplus this year, and that is up by some 33 per cent from last year. Naturally the Minister of of Finance (Mr. Chretien) was pleased and delighted with the figures that came out for the month of September. These are not abstract figures which do not fit back into every constituency of the country where we produce resources such as we do in the Algoma-Manitoulin area.
The Address-Mr. Foster
If we look at many of these resource items produced in that area we will see some positive and dramatic changes in the price and demand for those products. If we look at beef production, cow-calf operations, we will see prices this year up by some 75 per cent to 100 per cent over last year. At the annual sales in Thessalon and Little Current we saw a top price for 1977 of $51 per hundredweight for some 72 steer calves. This year at the fall sale in late September the price was $90.50 per hundredweight for some 60 steer calves. This is a very dramatic increase in the price of calves, following a period of some four years during which the producers of these calves suffered from extremely low prices, due in large part to the opportunities which exist for trade and sales to the United States as a result of the reduction in the value of the dollar. If this kind of price for the cow-calf operator can be maintained for the next several years, and there seems to be every indication this will happen, we will see a much more stable and positive industry there, one which has suffered very severely during the last few years. However, in respect of this year we observed the best price since 1974.
If we look at another sector of the resource industry, at lumber, for instance, we will see that we have had one of the strongest markets for lumber this year that we have experienced in many, many years. The demand is strong and prices are very high, certainly higher by at least $100 a thousand for two by fours and lumber products from many areas of northern Ontario than we have seen during the last 18 months. This industry is penetrating into markets in mid-western and eastern United States, and this is helping to push forward these high merchandise trade figures the Minister of Finance announced last week. The same situation exists in respect of newsprint and paper, so we are seeing a forest products industry in Canada that is in one of the strongest positions it has been in for many years.
In this connection I was pleased with the decision of the Minister of State (Environment) (Mr. Marchand) with regard to the Petawawa Forest Research Laboratory. I know the hon. member for Renfrew North-Nipissing East (Mr. Hopkins) has made tremendous representations in this regard. Many of us concerned with the forest products industry have, as well, made strong representations regarding the continuation of this research centre. The minister saw the wisdom of these arguments, and I understand that in fact the research centre will actually be increased in staff. I am pleased in this regard because it plays a vital and important role in the forest industry in Ontario, in the country and, in fact, in the world. This is important at this time because the Ontario government is changing over to having much of the reforestation, planting of seedlings, carried out by private companies in the pulp and paper industry. This kind of forest research will be very important in ensuring that this industry remains alive, well, and able to reach the full potential that our resources promise.
If we look at another sector of the resource industry, the uranium mining industry, putting aside the gloom and doom we hear from the other side of the aisle, we will see one of the strongest circumstances there in terms of trade opportunities

October 30, 1978
The Address-Mr. Foster
and expansion we have been able to visualize since 1958-59 when that industry was at its peak. In the Elliot Lake area of my constituency, for instance, there are two mining companies, Denison and Rio Algoma, expanding at a record rate, hiring literally hundreds of miners each year.
If we look at the difficulties in some other areas of the country and at our generally high unemployment figures throughout the country, we see that there is opportunity for young people and people interested in becoming miners. During the next six years it is expected that each of these companies will hire some 400 miners. We will see a community which today has some 15,000 people expanding to some
42.000	people. This is important in terms of jobs and economic development in that community, and it is important to our country as well. We are talking about literally billions of dollars in foreign exchange and in trade. This will offset our expenditures for oil and merchandise items which are imported into this country.
Canada has the uranium to sell, and the government has a policy to ensure that our needs will be met. One policy is that every reactor which is put on line must have a 40-year supply of uranium. At the same time we will be able to take advantage of the trade opportunities this important mineral will supply, and perhaps meet the energy needs of our trading partners, West Germany, Great Britain, Japan, United States, etc. It is therefore important that this mineral is further upgraded to its highest potential, and that is why it is government policy that the uranium to be exported from Canada is exported as uranium hexafluoride, a highly refined state.
There are hearings going on this fall with regard to the location of a new uranium refinery in the province of Ontario. It is my hope that it will be located in northern Ontario in the north shore area, and we in that area are trying to put forward a very positive case to have it located there. Last Saturday the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) visited Blind River to apprise himself of the advantages of locating the uranium refinery there. If such a thing occurs, it will provide some 240 permanent jobs, millions of dollars in assessment and capital investment in the community and will meet our desire there to further upgrade and process our natural uranium ore.
The greatest need in the rapidly expanding community of Elliot Lake right now is the need for housing. Each year there is a need for literally hundreds of new houses. Elliot Lake will grow from a population of 15,000 today to over 40,000 people in the next six or seven years. A whole new town will be developed during those years which will accommodate some
20.000	people. The existing property lots are being planned and developed at the present time. Surely, CMHC and the Department of Regional Economic Expansion will have a part to play in this expanded community, especially in providing houses for people in the service sector. The mining companies tend to look after their own quite well, but often there is a need for assistance from the government agencies to people in

the service sector, where the mining companies do not have a great responsibility.
Another industry that has been in a stronger position in the last year is the steel industry. I think the situation applies to the industry across Canada as well as to Algoma Steel at Sault Ste. Marie. The industry is operating at over 90 per cent capacity and is very close to 95 per cent of its capacity. If we compare our steel industry to that of Japan's, it is my understanding that they have had to shut down 22 of their 64 blast furnaces due to unused capacity.
The fact that our steel industry in Canada is in a very positive position is not something that can be taken for granted. Just a year or so ago Japan and several other countries were dumping steel on the Canadian market. A successful anti-dumping suit was brought against these companies and they have now moved back to a position where they are selling their steel in Canada at the same prices as the Canadian manufacturers. At the same time the Department of Finance and Department of National Revenue have established a benchmark procedure to assure that steel coming into the country is properly monitored so that there is no dumping.
If we look at the demands by the northern gas pipeline for steel, we can see that the market will improve in the years ahead. Just a few weeks ago the Foothills Pipeline company called tenders in the amount of 1.4 billion tons of steel. It is my understanding that during the next few weeks the Foothills company will be putting a procurement plan before the federal government and the minister responsible for the pipeline to assure that it meets all the needs of the Canadian market. I believe that we will see a continued strong situation in the steel industry in this country because of that pipeline, which will not only bring Prudhoe Bay gas to the lower 48 states, but will provide a transportation route for Canadian gas to the southern part of our country.
These are just four resource industries which are in a very strong position in our country. I hope that we recognize this as fact and do not listen to the doom and gloom we hear from the other side of the House.
It is important to note in the Speech from the Throne that significant incentives will be provided to the private sector during this coming year. Part of the strategy of the government in creating a healthy economy is to build on the strong industries we have today. The government intends to move back the level of government expenditure by $2.5 billion in order to let the private sector go forward.
At the same time the government recognizes that there are over 900,000 people unemployed in Canada today. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) has put together a program called "Strategy for Employment" which will provide some $710 million during the coming fiscal year to create 113,000 man-years of work and thus provide training and job opportunities for some 368,000 people.
An important thing about this, in my view, is that in addition to the 70 per cent increase in the number of jobs in
October 30, 1978

the next fiscal year this program will provide young people with some $225 million in the next fiscal year through, for example, the job experience training program. This was started last year and will utilize some unemployment insurance funds to give young people on the job experience in industry and in the private sector, while at the same time increasing the work force in the private sector. I want to congratulate the minister on that. It is an important strategy and one that has not been discussed enough.
Not only will that program operate all year round but there is as well a Young Canada Works program whose budget has been increased from $48 million to $62 million. Every year dozens of young people in communities enjoy the advantage of this program and the communities they serve enjoy the advantage of seeing their community projects carried out.
It seems to me that as we look at the Canadian scene today, although we see many economic problems we can also see a great number of positive things in the economy, in trade and in the resource industries. We should build on this and not whine about the difficulties we face. It is only by using the positive aspects of our economy to build on, both through the private sector and the direct job-creation programs of the government, that we will fulfil the great potential of this country.
After the vote tonight I believe we should get on with the business of this session of parliament. There is much positive and constructive legislation to be passed and we should pass it in a spirit of confidence so that we may reach the full potential that the resources of this country provide to us.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will try and condense my remarks as much as possible to comply with a wish by some official opposition members. First I would commend the mover and seconder of the address. The careful reader of the throne speech for this new session of the thirtieth parliament notes two priorities, the strengthening of our Canadian economy and the renewal of our federation, according to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). We are all agreed on the principle of a boost to the economy, but differences appear on the means of doing it. As concerns the renewal of our federation, we still do not have a clear notion of what the Prime Minister means by that phrase. A closest scrutiny might detect the dark ideas the Prime Minister is most jealously hiding from the people, his surprise box, so to speak. I shall come back to this in a few moments.
If we were to sum up in a very clear way the government's master thought in the throne speech and the legislative program, we might say it wants the provinces to pay the cost of its own mismanagement, taking this opportunity of a crisis of its own doing to take away from the provinces still more powers in order to reach its ultimate goal, the dictatorial federalism it has been trying to establish for ten years. When the Prime Minister refers to strengthening the economy, it is amazing how he sidesteps the issue of dealing with monopolies that affect the everyday life of Canadians, making them poorer by
The Address-Mr. Foster
the day, to the point it is normal these days to suggest the rich are getting bigger and bigger and the poor are getting smaller and smaller, and greater in numbers. When I discovered that before the 40's, workers paid no direct taxes, income tax in other words, I found that in those years big corporations paid 75 per cent of the national budget, which left only 25 per cent to collect from royalties or indirect taxes. Today, workers pay 75 per cent of the national budget while the big industrial and financial monopolies pay only 25 per cent, although their net revenues are ten times bigger than 40 years ago. It is therefore pointless to ask why workers are heavily burdened by federal taxes. The government proposes to reduce its expenditures, but this once more will be at the expense of small wage earners. Indeed, it is getting at those who cannot find work, the unemployed, people under welfare who have been denied benefits.
As always and according to a pre-conceived plan, the federal government will let the provincial governments support the burden of its mismanagement while keeping all the taxation rights and unemployment insurance premiums. The ministers are well aware that restricting eligibility for unemployment insurance and reducing the benefit period will cut down the number of recipients and proportionally increase the number of people on provincial welfare programs. The policy of this government is always to take more from the pay cheque of the worker and give him as little as possible. It keeps the provinces quiet by promising them to deal with such or such a sector to obtain the exclusive taxation rights in this area, and then it reneges on its promise while keeping the taxation rights obtained from the provinces. You will say that this is hypocrisy, but it is much more than that. It is treason! However, I do not want to go on any longer on this economic subject, but I shall probably come back to it during the budget debate.
I want to call the attention of parliament to a particular subject, the question of federalism. We must draw the attention of our young people to this notion of federalism. As for the renewal of federation, as it is called today-and I wonder why since it never really existed in Canada as we still have a confederation system-as for a renewal of the federation, the answer is certainly not in totally sterile discussions such as that which we witnessed in the House the other day between the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark). This discussion reminded me of a cock fight, and this assembly should be above such things. Such bickering is of no use to the Canadian people who would rather have more information and more details about the political and economic direction of our country.
In the few minutes allotted to me, I would like to appeal to the intelligence of those members who want to leave the paths of petty politics on which many have ventured during the debates of this House since the first mention of an election. It is very important first of all to see where we are today. For ten
614

October 30, 1978
The Address-Mr. Foster
years, the Prime Minister and his government have repeated the words profitable federalism; they have said that we need a strong central government for a united Canada, and so on, and suggested that those who want to oppose this extremist policy which is a fore runner of the bureaucratic dictatorship that we have repeatedly denounced, are destructors of Canada or even separatists. Even the proposal of a third solution by the Pepin-Robarts Commission had no merit in the eyes of the Prime Minister who believes that he alone holds the true solution.
Mr. Speaker, I believe there should be an end to this verbal battle. The Prime Minister is trying to stir up a war between the provinces which want only one thing, that is to be given back the direct taxation right guaranteed under the British North America Act, which ensures their autonomy or their sovereignty, if you prefer, the base of the confederation created in 1867. I wonder if the greatest separatist nowadays is not the Prime Minister of Canada, because of his intransigence and his harshness towards the provinces. And to give the population an idea of the importance of the debate opening today, it is enough to define "confederation" and "federalism." These definitions are of major importance for all Canadians who will have to make a decision on the form of government of the future. Until now, the old political parties have played so much with words to delude the public and try to impose their ideology that the public wonders where it stands in regard with the 1867 confederation. Canadians seriously wonder if the words still retain their original meaning because the politicians have distorted them so much. Mr. Speaker, this is no time for confrontation but for negotiation. What is a confederation? I come now to it's definition. According to the dictionary a confederation is a union of sovereign, hence independent and autonomous states. That is the kind of confederation the Fathers of Confederation wanted. At least that is the meaning given to confederation in the dictionary. That is quite clear. So why does the Prime Minister call separatists all those who claim that sovereignty for the provinces and Quebec in particular? Is he denying that right of the provinces to sovereignty? That is exactly what the Fathers of Confederation wanted in all freedom in 1867, and that is what we should have in Canada today.
Had that confederation not been polluted by the ever increasing appetite of the federal government which resulted in the provinces being robbed of 50 per cent of their rights in the past 110 years we would not be having that fight to recover provincial rights guaranteed by the British North America Act, that sovereignty which was the essential condition of the confederative pact of 1867, with freedom of choice. Why has the Liberal government been trying for the past ten years to deny both? The evidence is there, and all governments since 1867 have recognized that undeniable fact. That sovereignty was always respected in spite of all the compromises reached at federal-provincial conferences. Indeed, even in 1942, that

sovereignty was confirmed by the government of the time and recognized by all political parties in the House. In support of that, I refer those who want to read it to the schedule attached to the draft agreement of 1942. For ten years the Prime Minister has been waging the fight for federalism which he does not want to define to enlighten somewhat the people in that maze where he wants to keep them.
Mr. Speaker, I have here a few paragraphs of that agreement of 1942. You know that the province of Quebec gave up with the other provinces its rights to direct taxation on account of the war, and 1 quote:
Whereas it is necessary that the federal parliament alone have the power to levy direct taxes on incomes and corporations to allow Canada to give a maximum effort in the pursuit of the present war;
Whereas the federal government is willing to pay adequate compensation to the province provided it agrees not to levy such taxes for the duration of the war;
Whereas the federal government recognizes that the province, in agreeing to do so, does not in any way give up or cede any part of its sovereignty or any of its constitutional rights, powers and privileges;
That seems clear to me. Those who want to read that agreement will see that the federal government recognized the sovereignty of the provinces and also respected it. And furthermore, it agreed to respect it. Mr. Speaker, that is what the Fathers of Confederation wanted in all liberty in 1867, and that is what we would like to see today in Canada. Why then make it a crime for a province to want to recover that sovereignty? I think we will see a good example of it when time comes to discuss monetary matters with the other provinces. They will want to hang on to their monetary sovereignty.
What is that federalism the right hon. Prime Minister would implement through force? I say "force" because not one province agrees with the government, and the best proof of it is what we saw in the last elections. Let us count what is left of the Liberal government in the provinces and we will have even better proof when time comes to discuss jurisdictions and the sharing of powers on the economic level. I want that definition to be remembered.
What is federalism? According to the dictionary it is a political system in which several independent and sovereign states relinquish a part of their sovereignty to a supreme state. It is quite clear. I think that is the idea that the right hon. Prime Minister has in mind. In fact, the provinces will have to sacrifice their sovereignty to the benefit of a strong central government. And the Prime Minister confirms my assumptions when he declares in his legislative program that "the new constitution must provide that Canada will remain a true federation." Is it possible in Canada? It might be possible when two nations are living in the same unified country and one of them is assimilated by the other; but I think this situation does not prevail in Canada as Lord Durham's prediction did not come true yet. The English provinces, also keeping a jealous watch over their economic sovereignty, have just proved it by rejecting the Liberal party in all their provinces. The province of Quebec is adult enough to make its own
October 30, 1978

decision about its future. When I hear charges of separatism, it reminds me of the fall of 1970 when the government saw the FLQ everywhere but forgot to check within its own party, its own departments and its own police force.
I prefer to believe that the present government will consider the provinces as autonomous states by giving them back their property taxes that are direct taxes, so that they can manage their own affairs. We recognize that every province is different and that in Quebec this difference is even more acute because of its language, its common law, its institutions and what have you. This is why we do not believe in unity but in harmony between Canadian nations. This is what we believe and what we propose.
Mr. Speaker, the right hon. Prime Minister declares for the hundredth time his desire to make Canada a united country with a strong central government, that is to make the people accept the bureaucratic dictatorship he has imposed on us in the last ten years. The Liberal party is continually proclaiming that the Quebec government was not elected to separate Canada and, in my view, that party answers by moving towards negotiation. But we want to tell the Prime Minister that neither was he elected to establish a dictatorship in Canada. The worst is that he knows what he is doing, and where he is going while he is shouting to Mr. Levesque to explain clearly his sovereignty-association theory. Does the Prime Minister define clearly what his federalism means? He takes care not to do so, Mr. Speaker.
On our side, we want the government to tell the Canadian people how it defines federalism. Does the Prime Minister tell the people that his federalism is defined in the dictionary? Everyone noticed that he never says the word confederation. However this is what we want, and the 1867 union was a confederation, which was a bit of a sham, but it is what the four provinces at that time, which were still British colonies, wanted. They even gave birth to the federal government in all freedom, after consulting each other.
When I was a schoolboy they always praised the merits of , the Fathers of Confederation. But as adults, we lived the reality of this confederative union. Today, we admit that the Fathers of Confederation had perhaps good intentions but it is not enough to establish a free country. We went through the sad experience of a colonized country, with all the underlying consequences, and this reality still haunts the minds of several of our older people.
This is why we want a renewal but this time it is wanted by us, a constitution written by the provinces clearly indicating the fields of activity that they would grant to the federal government which would become a creature of the provinces, that is what is was at the beginning, working in sectors well defined by the provinces such as currency, defence, external affairs, post office etc., those provisions being accepted at first under a provincial referendum to be ratified by a second national referendum.
The Address-Mr. Malone
Such is the position of our party, Mr. Speaker, a position which we have always championed and which we continue to champion to restore Canadian harmony. I am convinced that if we do not take a step in that direction, we will be led to disaster. I therefore ask each citizen to consider thoroughly the national issue leaving aside for a moment his partisanship to choose the form of government he seeks.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to commence in the traditional way by extending my thanks to the mover and seconder of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I do not do so because it is the tradition that we do it to newer members of this chamber, but because I believe they distinguished themselves in their content and in their eloquence.
Before getting into my remarks, I wish to state that I feel a very deep sense of uniqueness about today. While different members have spoken on national unity in this country, in the government and opposition lobbies we have been watching over television the first ministers' conference.
There are some tremendous debates on the various views and opinions in the country, in this House and across the street as to how this country ought to be forged together. In that vein, I wish the first ministers great wisdom. I hope they will have a far-sighted vision and genuine compassion for the regions of Canada. This is a very important day. All members will want to extend to them best wishes on what could be a very historical deliberation.
We are at a place in our history where we must give serious consideration as to how we are going to unite ourselves. This question of national unity has been surrounded with many myths which have been perpetuated by those who would like to put national unity in front of the Canadian people as a red herring in order to divert their attention from the real issues facing this nation.
Until Bill C-60 came before the House of Commons last spring, not a single constituent ever asked me about the Constitution of Canada and why it was not changed. In my four years as a member of parliament, in fact in the previous 30 to 40 years, there has not been a single bill, regulation or piece of legislation that has somehow been denied by the present constitution.
Some myths and falsehoods are being perpetuated by the present government. One was reiterated this morning by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) in his opening speech. He said that Canada does not have a constitution and that we have been trying to get one for some 50 years. He went on to say that no other nation in the world is in the situation Canada is in of not having a constitution.
We do have a constitution. It is defined as the British North America Act. Canadians from the Atlantic to the Pacific are fully aware that it is our constitution, that it belongs to us. It is unfortunate that it is implied that somehow we are a lesser
80065-401/:!

October 30, 1978
The Address-Mr. Malone
nation because we are not guided by some piece of paper and that we are thereby a colony of Great Britain.
Although our constitution came to us in a different form than did that of the United States, we do have a constitution. Having said that, I want to say this is a momentous day. The task is not that of writing a constitution for Canada. The task is trying to improve that which we already have.
There is another important idea which must be underscored at this time. There can be nothing terminal in the date of July 1, 1979. The Prime Minister has said that by the date the constitution of Canada must be passed or put in a form that is to his likeness. Obviously, it must have the greatest of deliberation. It must not be tied to a timetable simply to enable the Prime Minister to achieve his ultimate end of taking his place in history as the one who established constitutional reform in Canada. That is a dangerous program to follow. To take something so fundamental as the constitution and to put a time frame on it is to embark on a dangerous course.
Constitutions by their nature guide the very way in which we live. Whether it be a constitution for a youth organization, company or manufacturing organization, club or association, or for the government of the country, it is simply a piece of paper, a document to guide how we will act one toward another.
The government has chosen the wrong time to bring the constitution question into focus. Groups and societies decide how they will act together when they are in a state of harmony. What we have today is a country torn apart, a country that is divided, a country that is unemployed, that has no work, that lacks production, has a $50 billion debt and in every way has created tensions on language, cultural, ethnic and economic grounds. It is in that milieu that the Prime Minister is trying to say that we will formulate a constitution for ourselves and decide how we will relate to one another for however long Canada shall be. It is in that messy, ugly chicken coop that the Prime Minister, acting as the fox, is trying to preach national unity.
If we look, then, at some of the issues on which we note that division has taken place, we find there has been confrontation with the provinces, an assumption of unilateral powers by the federal government, and a desire to treat the Queen like some kind of Christmas tree ornament. Our balance of trade has significantly decreased, the value of the dollar is down, we have seen a 230 per cent increase in government spending, and the phasing out of small vessel insurance on the Pacific and Atlantic coasts which makes the workers feel that somehow less attention is being given to their concerns and needs.
The most dangerous threat to unity is to talk about unity at a time when you have not established common goals. I would submit that one of the most dangerous things we could be doing is talking about national unity at the very time when there is this sense of stress in the nation. We might even say that one of the greatest dangers to national harmony itself is the perpetual dominance of talk about unity. A country could

well be like a marriage; if all we are going to do is talk about the things that make us different, obviously harmony cannot be found.
When you have common goals and common objectives, that is when you grow together, as was truly evident in this country in 1967 when Expo brought this nation together. It was clearly evident in the first hockey game between Canada and the Soviet Union, when we acted from our hearts as one. But it is clearly not the case today when, after ten years of this government's mismanagement, we see people divided, thinking in different ways. I believe strongly that the proper approach to national unity is to recreate for this country a common set of objectives, common drives, common aspirations. After a sense of goodwill has been developed in all regions of the country, we can then sit down in a spirit of mutual co-operation and hammer out the kind of nation we want to have.
Expanding some of the comments I was making when I said the Prime Minister had divided this nation, I would like to underscore some of the ways in which I believe he has very deliberately, I would say, cast an injustice upon my part of the country, namely western Canada. Two years ago they purchased from our side of the House a man to go to sit with them as a cabinet minister. That person was somehow to be the guardian of the province of Alberta in the cabinet. After going through the list of injustices which have been done to the province of Alberta, I can only conclude that sending the Minister of Inudstry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) to guard Alberta against Liberals is analagous only to sending an alley cat to guard mice.
Let us take a look at some of the detrimental things that have happened to the province of Alberta. If anyone is in any way intending to protect that province from the government, there is every reason to believe he simply is not being effective. We note that construction of the Lethbridge Research Laboratory has been cancelled. We note that the contribution toward the construction of a veterinary university has been cancelled; students from that large livestock producing province must now migrate to another province in order to get that style of education. The Canfarm program has been canned, together with the Canadian Dairy Commission's allocation for product research.
I think that is important, because this is a party which believes in trimming the fat from the budget. But much of what we are talking about here deals with the very kind of incentives that will increase the production of the country. The Farm Credit Corporation has suffered a reduction of some $23 million and there is no group of people in the nation today anywhere, by the admission of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), which has a better record for production and per capita output than does the farming population. Again, the forestry research stations are very closely related to production. Several of those were intended to be closed. The only ones that got reopened happened to be those in Liberal ridings; somehow the heat from back home warmed up some of the cabinet ministers.
October 30, 1978

How else, Mr. Speaker, would Alberta have felt recognizing that, when they wanted to make a natural gas trade with the United States in relation to some beef imports, the heavy hand of the Minister of Agriculture prevented it? How else would they act when there is a sales tax rebate program for every province except Alberta, and they do not get in on those federal cookies because somehow it looks to them like a Liberal barren wasteland? So they simply turn an ignoring eye. How were they supposed to act when the public utilities income tax transfer act made changes which most significantly affected Alberta? Because utilities in that province are largely privately-owned and therefore will not be part of this particular program. Take the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce where they cut $9 million from marketing incentive programs and imposed a reduction in assistance for grains and oil seed marketing. Obviously, there are places where government can cut. I do not want to get on record as saying I do not think we should make cuts. But there are in excess of 360 Crown corporations, many of which could easily be put up for individual Canadians to buy shares in, much along the lines Alberta did with the Alberta Gas Trunk Lines; thus Canadians could invest in their own resources and take over some of these top-heavy government agencies which could easily go back into private hands.
We note that in transportation, market research, forestry and agricultural research, the area of assisting people in production, the very areas in which we are failing as a nation economically, the government has decided to cut back. One does not have to be an economist or need to have a very high education or a great sense of wisdom to take that blue book of expenditures off the shelf and turn through the pages and cut far more than the $2 billion the government cut without directly injuring areas which significantly affect the productivity of the nation.
My opponent in the next election has put out little match boxes in the riding which say "Re-elect an effective voice in Ottawa". All I know is that after the damage which has been done to the province by Ottawa we do not want effective voices down here, because every time we get them we lose. We heard that before when Pat Mahoney was here; we got the capital gains tax. I submit that is one of the most retrograde taxes which could be imposed on a democratic society. Democracies, in order to work, require a strong middle class. Capital gains taxes do not tax the poor because they do not make money, and they do not tax the rich corporations because they do not sell. General Motors does not sell, and IBM does not sell. Such companies do not therefore get into the position of having to pay capital gains tax.
But the owner of the local barber shop, small businessmen generally, are in a different position. To every generation of such people the government comes for its pound of flesh. It is a very dangerous aspect of our tax system in light of the fact that this is the part of society which creates the largest percentage of wealth, something like 55 per cent, and the largest share of employment, about 80 per cent. The government somehow thinks it has to go after that sector with the
The Address-Mr. Malone
capital gains tax because it wants universality regarding retirement funds. The government would rather tax people and then put them on government pensions than give them incentives to produce.
I mentioned that Ottawa picks on the regions. It uses a sledgehammer to drive shingle nails. It has made cuts in an attempt to fool the public. The government claims it wants to cut back, but a serious analysis would show that there is no such intention. The cuts made were in the most popular programs in an attempt to get the public and the opposition angry so that later they will demand that those programs be reinstated. That would give the Prime Minister the opportunity to shrug his shoulders and say, "I tried to make cuts, but they did not like them". Then he will continue his rampant spending.
Transportation is seriously inadequate in all parts of the country. I began today by talking about national unity. I submit that one of the most important aspects regarding national unity is an improved transportation system. The inequities which exist in the present system cause one region to be angry with all or some regions of the country. Potatoes from Atlantic Canada often reach their destinations 30 per cent frozen because of a lack of insulated cars. Products from the prairies are not getting to market, yet this government allows 23,000 grain cars to be on loan to the United States because there is a better dollar for them down there.
We need to develop infrastructures which would give us a productivity level which would get our balance of payments back on track, but the reserves is the situation. For example, the government decided to sell five inland grain terminals which were underutilized. Even though they were underutilized, they had been making profits in the previous several years. The Hall commission report strongly recommended that those elevators not be sold but, rather, upgraded and utilized more. It is important that we recognize that grain should be dried and cleaned on the prairies prior to being taken to market. That has been talked about since the Western Economic Opportunities Conference. That conference was called because in 1972 the government lost four Liberal members in the province of Alberta, and the Prime Minister wanted to find out what Alberta really wanted.
The Western Economic Opportunities Conference brought great promise. It underscored many transportation requirements. It underscored many regional disparities regarding production. However, nothing was done. After that conference the Hall and Snavely commissions were set up. Those two commissions outlined palatable and acceptable recommendations as far as westerners were concerned, and western producers were encouraged, but the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) then set up another commission to study the recommendations of the first two commissions. The people of this country are getting tired of studies to find out what other studies mean. They want a government which is committed to

October 30, 1978
The Address-Mr. Malone
action which will right the inequities which exist and which will give them some sense of direction.
This government wears masks. It appointed an ombudsman for the Ministry of Transport, for whom there is no need. That is an absolute waste of money. The A-uditor General is assigned the task of checking on various departments. Any well managed government department does not need an ombudsman. We may well need ombudsmen at the federal and provincial levels to act as clearing houses for citizens at large, but surely not at the departmental level. This kind of ombudsman concept smacks of a government which is admitting its incapacity to govern.
This government sold five elevators in an attempt to trim its budget, yet the elevators were making money for the federal treasury.
The government built a railway to Churchill, Manitoba, using 100-pound steel except for the last few miles, where it used 80 pound steel. Therefore, the only trains which can be used for the whole length of the track are trains which have loads no heavier than that which can travel on 80-pound steel. That is the kind of ineffective mismanagement that we have.
The government talks about increasing storage capacity at the terminals at the port of Churchill, yet we note that this year the port of Churchill was underutilized by some nine million bushels. The government talks about selling more grain abroad, yet it allows 23,000 grain cars to be on loan in the United States. The result is reduced productivity.
Mr. Speaker, I see that hon. members opposite are either sleepy or hungry, so I will call it six o'clock.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to the hon. member who has yielded his right to speak. I will try to be as brief as possible since there are many hon. members who wish to take part in the debate.
Last year I had the honour to be one of the movers of the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne. I therefore seize this opportunity to congratulate the hon. member for

York South (Mrs. Appolloni) for the outstanding distinction with which she performed that task. As for the seconder, the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Savard), I found it significant that he emphasized in his speech the difficulties senior citizens are up against in our society of today. Besides, I did point out in my speech last year the circumstances of the young, the old and the low income people. The federal government has done much in these areas but, like the hon. member for Verdun, I feel that it will have to intensify those programs.
Mr. Speaker, in the few minutes which I am being granted, I will attempt once again to raise the questions contained in the speech I delivered last year in the House of Commons and to assess the extent of government action in this respect.
Among the issues which I brought to the attention of the House last year was the economic development of the Quebec region. On that specific issue, I want to congratulate the government for the contribution it made to the development of the Quebec harbour by dredging the channel of the Saint-Laurent River so as to lower its level from 38 to 41 feet.
This year the government went one step further. The Department of Transports has already commissioned a study dealing with the construction of a wood product shipping harbour for the Quebec area.
Moreover we should mention the development project in the harbour of the old city of Quebec which was announced on February 13 this year during the travelling caucus of which I was chairman and which brought together five ministers and a dozen members from Quebec and Ontario into the riding of Louis-Hebert and the Quebec region.
Announced by the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), Quebec city's old harbour development project implies numerous and significant benefits on the economic development of the area. This $42 million federal program spread over four years is designed to give a new life to some 179 acres of federal acreage located in Quebec city's old harbour district. It will involve the relocation of some industrial, harbour and railway facilities that are now antiquated and do not belong in the urban and historical environment surrounding them. These facilities would be replaced by cultural, leisure and social services, as well as residential and administrative buildings.
However, I must insist that this should be only the beginning of harbour development in the Quebec city area because its harbour is in competition with other ports on the St. Lawrence River, on the Atlantic as well as the western coast. The Quebec city metropolitan area already has a good railway and road system allowing for the quick transportation of goods to the large centres. The Quebec city area offers tremendous potential, and I believe it is essential to develop its harbour.
In this vein of economic development in the Quebec city region, Mr. Speaker, the extension of its airport is a second priority which I dealt with in my speech last year. A few
October 30, 1978

months ago, the Minister of Transport made announcements in this regard. First, the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Lapointe), acting as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport, answered my question regarding the extension of runways. He announced in the House that in view of Quebec City's hotel accommodation and convention facilities, and I quote:
-it becomes more and more urgent to extend the present runway. This is why the minister intends to ask very soon for the necessary funds to extend the runway to 9,000 feet. We hope that the amounts will be invested in the area at the very beginning of summer.
Then, in August, 1978, at a press conference held jointly with representatives of the chamber of commerce and industry of metropolitan Quebec city, the Department of Transport tabled a master plan for the development of the airport over the next ten years.
The master plan of the Quebec airport provides for the extension of one of the two runways to 2743 metres, that is 9,000 feet, in order to accommodate big jets; the building of boarding ramps to be announced shortly; the addition of another storey to the air terminal in order to build a restaurant; and finally, the eventual separation of commercial traffic from small craft training flights and general aviation. That plan, which has been approved by the Department of Transport, is the result of joint studies and consultations by all interested organizations in the Quebec area, including the air companies and the Association des Gens de l'air. It is designed mainly to meet the increasing needs of the Quebec region and to promote the tourist industry in that area.
The national unity issue was also raised in the debate last year and again this year. It was dealt with according to the highlights of the Speech from the Throne made about two weeks ago.
I also know that the government's primary objective is to give back to the country a sense of unity. It is seeking solutions by consulting all individuals and all agencies or groups concerned about the country's future. Moreover, we cannot ignore the fact that we are all affected by the national unity crisis no matter what hon. members of the opposition say. We all know that economic prosperity will not be of a great use to us if we lose our country through internal quarrels and Quebec's separation.
In a very real sense, Mr. Speaker, national unity should remain our first subject of concern. We owe it to ourselves to pursue our search and to keep conceiving new policies and new strategies. We have to create the blend of collective will and individual attitudes that will allow all Canadians to feel at home everywhere in Canada and to participate in all justice and plenitude in the life and prosperity of the country.
To solve the problems that threaten the stability, the unity and the prosperity of our country, a fundamental renewal of the federation of Canada is imperative. At this turning point in the history of our country, we have a unique opportunity to
reaffirm our basic values and adjust our practices, our institu-
The Address-Mr. Dawson tions and our constitution to modern realities.
Further to its commitment, in June last the federal government tabled a white paper entitled "A Time for Action", which traces the main steps towards renewal of the Canadian federation, and Bill C-60 on the constitutional reform. Canadians, and more so Quebeckers, have surely been able to see that the government of Canada is in earnest, and that it does not deal in abstract notions such as the so-called sovereignty-association.
The government attempts to define an orientation, to prove, once more, Mr. Speaker, its will to come up with negotiable proposals. We saw that again this afternoon when the federal government made proposals. All the prime ministers of the provinces stressed the fact that the matter was not necessarily urgent. This afternoon, we heard from the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson) and the hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Malone).
To that end, the government set up a special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons on the constitution of Canada. That committee, which was instructed to study and report on the proposals which have been made and will be made public at a later date by the Canadian government on matters pertaining to the constitution of Canada, heard several witnesses, individuals as well as organizations, all of whom are concerned with the constitutional renewal.
As one of the representatives of the House of Commons on that committee, I was in a position to see how necessary the reform of the constitution is, except perhaps in the eyes of a few hon. members.
Thus the need for a new constitution is a major necessity if we are to try to keep Quebec and Quebeckers in confederation. The dilemma with which we are faced is not simple. As professor Leon Dion of Laval University said in his brief before the committee:
Therefore, we have to decide whether it would be better to carry out the revision of the Constitution immediately without the participation of the Quebec government or whether on the contrary the whole matter should be postponed as long as Quebec, through a referendum or otherwise, would not have succeeded in expressing a unanimous opinion. By waiting for Quebec we risk causing a serious delay in the reshaping of the country, but by acting without Quebec we risk doing useless work and reaping sour grapes.
This dilemma is not simple and, if we add to it the resistance we have seen to the first propositions of the government, our task is far from finished.

This year's Speech from the Throne delivered by the Governor General mentions that the government is prepared to begin the study of the distribution of powers and jurisdictions at the same time as that of institutions and rights, and to give every aspect of the work a high and urgent priority. Even after meeting that request, Mr. Speaker, we saw once again this afternoon at the first ministers' conference that this is not

October 30, 1978
The Address-Mr. Dawson
enough for the province of Quebec or the other provinces. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the government of Canada should show once again a great flexibility and a great deal of good faith.
On the other hand, I am happy to see the increased importance the government attaches these days to the problems of unemployment among young people. The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) defined last week a score of programs to bring young people into the labor market through grants for the hiring of new graduates and young unemployed graduates. Those programs are intended to provide jobs for about 58,000 unemployed youths. Once again, we saw in the Speech from the Throne the importance the government attaches to that priority, namely the problem of unemployment among young people. And I quote from the Speech:
The major thrust of the government's employment strategy is to encourage the creation of permanent jobs in the private sector. Special emphasis is being placed on the training and job placement of young Canadians.
The problem of unemployment among young people is not acute only in Canada; it exists in most western countries. I hope the government of Canada with its new measures will continue to show leadership in its fight against that plague. Mr. Speaker, let me say in concluding that after more than a year in the House of Commons I am proud to be part of this group of parliamentarians-with a few exceptions, I must admit-trying to help Canadians save this country regardless of their origin and their affiliations. I am proud to be part of this government and I am proud to represent and serve the people of the riding of Louis-Hebert from this side of the House.

speechtext: 1 recognize the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Shymko). I should like to point out to hon. members that this is the hon. member's maiden speech.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before making any comment on the debate on the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne opening the fourth session of the thirtieth parliament, I would like first to reaffirm one feeling and indeed one reality related to the fact that I am here as a member of the House of Commons, among this elite, this distinguished assembly, distinguished because of its speakers, its leaders and sometimes because of its actors.
First I speak of that feeling. Mr. Speaker, 25 years ago, as a youngster of 13, I arrived here in Canada as a political immigrant with my parents. Having survived hatred, war and death as one of the survivors from Dresden-everybody has heard and knows about the tragedy in that city-I came to this country of dream, of peace, of liberty and justice, and I am
now among you as a member. That is possible only in a country like Canada. I must remind hon. members, Mr. Speaker, that I did not have to change my name Yuri for George and Shymko for Simcoe to achieve that. I hope that this country, where such a rare opportunity exists in a world of prejudices and intolerance, will continue to represent the dream, the hope, the optimism of knowing that what is impossible in other countries is still possible in Canada. That is possible because of the people, because of the moral and individual values which form the political, economic and social framework in which we as leaders are operating and which we must protect at any cost.
Referring to the second reality, Mr. Speaker, it is a fact inconsistent with all speculations, projections and political prophecies of those experts who predicted that the representative of the governing party would win the by-election in the Parkdale fortress. Well, here I am. I am not a ghost and what you see is real and possible, a prophetic indication for the spring of 1979 of which hon. members opposite are well aware.
It was Pascal, the great French philosopher who said: "The heart has its reasons which reason knows nothing of." Well, Mr. Speaker, the Parkdale constituents have shown their feelings when they voted against all the arguments of the media and political experts, in spite of two personal visits of the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Trudeau), in spite of the constant visits of the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik). When they voted they showed their feeling, their compassion for this country, their love for that politically polarized, divided and as we know, economically bankrupt country. I will not quote any statistics, you have heard enough statistics given by my colleagues on this side of the House. This is why I decided to give my first speech in the House and I wish to comment on the following paragraph taken from the Speech from the Throne:
We wish also to express our love of Canada. A great country is not created without difficulty, but to see it develop and grow stronger despite every obstacle has been for us a source of great joy and pride. Our faith in the future of Canada is stronger than it has ever been.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to speak of that love and faith.
I, too, will not be partisan, like the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo (Mr. Jamieson), the minister for external affairs, and I will try to digress somehow from the normal procedure. I will speak of the essence of our function as members of parliament and of our common responsibilities as servants of the people on whatever side of this House we sit. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has said, "Canada grows stronger." It reminds me of the cliche of the past campaigns, "The land is strong." He has also said, "Our faith in Canada is stronger than it has ever been."
Let us look at the growing strength of Canada under the management, or more appropriately, the mismanagement, of this government. What kind of strength do we have with one million unemployed, a diminishing manufacturing industry

October 30, 1978

which, in fact, makes Canada a warehouse for imported manufactured products, with a Canadian dollar at its lowest base-lower than the worst period of the depression-with a standard of living that has fallen from second to seventh place in the world? How can the Prime Minister call Canada strong with a $15 billion deficit that is growing every day? How can Canada be considered strong when the government proposes a bill to borrow $17 billion to save the country from total bankruptcy? I could spend the next hour listing the Liberal interpretations of strength. If this is strength, I cannot imagine what the Liberal definition for a weak economy is.
The right hon. member for Mount Royal spoke about faith. We could see examples of that faith in our economy when 1.7 billion of Canada's dollars have left this country in the past three years, when the Prime Minister himself had to go to Germany to be "Schmidt-en" with the wisdom of realizing that the priority of this land is the economy. The proposals of Her Majesty's opposition to cut government spending by $2 billion were the best and the only options that made any sense. Ask and ye shall be given; the government asked and the opposition certainly gave the answers.
But above all, it represents one basic truth, that the government has lost its moral prestige and its moral authority in Canada and now wants to use its sole legal authority to make this fourth session an electioneering session to save face before its citizens. It will, indeed, be a tragedy if the government turns this session into an election campaign. If we do this it will destroy the very aim of parliament-to rule and to legislate, to serve, not to manipulate the hopes and needs of people. The function of parliament as I understood it before being elected, and as I still understand it, is not to become a pompous circus for the entertainment of others or for selfgratification. If such is the aim of the government, it would be much better to accept the reality, as many ministers have themselves admitted, that people in Canada have had enough. They are protesting, as illustrated by the results of the by-elections. The people want a change and there is nothing wrong with changing sides on the floor of this House. We do it as individuals and as gentlemen every day between debates, and all we need do now is to do it collectively.
The Prime Minister likes to pick on the opposition, as was illustrated last week when he colourfully referred to the posterior of a member of the opposition and wanted to kick that particular part of his anatomy. I admit it was quite an introduction to the House of Commons, to be here when that famous remark was made. It was interesting that it was the only remark that made the media. In the confusion I thought that the Prime Minister was referring to expanding his cabinet by picking another member of the opposition, following the example of the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner).
Getting back to my earlier point, we can talk about love and faith, but we cannot legislate love and faith. Just as we cannot legislate tolerance, respect for the dignity of man and respect for law, we cannot legislate confidence in this land, confidence in this economy, confidence in this government and faith in our future. How can the government expect respect for the law
The Address-Mr. Shymko
from workers they have legislated back to work when, on the other hand, rumours and insinuations are rampant throughout this country that even some ministers of the Crown were tampering with illegalities? The government is responsible to the people and to parliament; the hon. member for Winnipeg South (Mr. Richardson) pointed this out this afternoon.
Lawmakers must be subjected to the rule of law, not to the rule of manifest unilateral authority. The Prime Minister, if he has not seen it by now, must stop moulding Canada in terms of the shape of his own ideas; he must change his views and values to reflect those of this nation and of the majority of its people. As for the question of unity, it would require another hour at least to adequately discuss this issue.
I would like to refer to the comments made today by the Secretary of State for External Affairs-

-who states that as a former citizen of Newfoundland before that province joined our Canadian confederation a few years ago, he was a foreigner and that he now considers himself completely Canadian.
Mr. Speaker, what is most tragic is that at the time the minister joined the rest of Canada, Quebeckers felt strongly that they were Canadians, while today many of them-and the number is increasing-feel more and more like strangers in this vast country, which was in the past a country of great dreams and great visions and where they enthusiastically celebrated their centennial 11 years ago, united in their hopes and beliefs for the future. But today, Canada is divided, polarized and torn by fear and suspicion. A great number of studies have analysed this situation and suggested solutions. I simply want to say that the question of unity, the problems that it causes or the means to solve them are not as simple as we would want them to be. Everyone of us, Mr. Speaker, every party, every member of parliament, every government leader, whether federal or provincial, and every Canadian, whatever his cultural background, will need to make a great effort of understanding, tolerance and sacrifice if we are to solve this problem.
Let us compare this with the case of Newfoundland. There is only one point that I want to make; if in its historical evolution, Quebec has progressed toward a responsible, parliamentary and democratic government with a blossoming of collective and individual rights, if in its efforts towards the creation of a French-speaking nation in North America, as other colonies in North and South America which have gained their own independence, if Quebec had been autonomous like Newfoundland until the second part of this century, I am certain that it would find it much easier now to join this Canadian federation after having tasted independence. It is the lack of this second stage in its history which now troubles the French-speaking nation. But if we see Canada, like Laurier, as a cathedral still in the process of being built, as a courageous experiment-

October 30, 1978
The Address-Mr. Shymko
-by a segment of humanity in a world where majorities destroy and persecute minorities; in a world where hatred and wars, injustice, the destruction of civil, human and national liberties are the rule, where democracies are the privileges of only one-fifth of the world's population. Let us not destroy this dream, let us not destroy this vision.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Let us build it with all the determination, all the faith, all the confidence, all the love and respect for one another that is at our disposal. Because I, as well as millions of Canadians, be they Anglophones, Francophones, or "neither-phones", still cherish this dream.
There is nothing wrong with bill 101, given a few revisions. There is nothing wrong with a referendum in Quebec, given that the majority of Quebecois, as I firmly believe, will speak out for unity, will speak for this confederation of regions, of peoples and of cultures. What is wrong is our indifference. What is wrong is our suspicion, our fears and, above all, our lack of confidence in ourselves that we can indeed "make it".
What is wrong is not that the Quebecois have taken over the civil service because they are the only bilingual segments of our population. What is wrong is that today only 43 per cent of high school students in such a great province as Ontario even bother to study French and that less than 5 per cent complete Grade 13.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Right on!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Tell Bill Davis about that!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The reason for this, Mr. Speaker, as well as the changes that are made in Quebec where the study of English was obligatory, is the fact that it was made an option, just as the study of French had been obligatory when I came to this country, a time when the crisis of unity did not exist. It was obligatory, but when the issue in this country became polarized, French was made an option. Now, no one bothers to study French, and the same trend is beginning in Quebec.
Let us not point to the premier of Ontario or to anyone in particular. As I said earlier, this is the responsibility of every Canadian, of every prime minister and of every premier of every province.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Finally, Mr. Speaker, let me conclude by referring again to the question of faith and love. Only the person who has faith in himself is able to have faith in others and is able to be faithful to others. In no other period in the history of this country has faith in ourselves been so diminished, so troubled, as in the last decade. Hon. members, Mr. Speaker, can deduce the reasons for themselves.
Faith is a condition of our ability to promise. As a condition of human existence, faith in the potentialities of others, the potentialities of government in particular, is slowly being eroded. Indeed, for one particular government very little is left.
As for love, Mr. Speaker, I should like to end my speech by quoting from a pocket book entitled "The Art of Loving". It does not deal with a subject that some hon. members would like to hear about. The author of this pocket book is Erich Fromm. At page 111, he has this to say:
Our society is run by a managerial bureaucracy, by professional politicians; people are motivated by mass suggestion, their aim is producing more and consuming more, as purposes in themselves. All activities are subordinated to economic goals, means have become ends; man is an automaton-well fed, well clad, but without any ultimate concern for that which is his peculiarly human quality and function. If man is to be able to love, he must be put in his supreme place. The economic machine must serve him, rather than he serve it. He must be enabled to share experience, to share work, rather than, at best, share in profits. Society must be organized in such a way that man's social, loving nature is not separated from his social existence, but becomes one with it.
This is my conclusion, Mr. Speaker. It may have been a little philosophical but in the future 1 hope to have the opportunity to dwell on topics the surface of which I have just touched tonight. I thank this country for the honour and the privilege of being here with you and working with you for many months, if not many years. God bless you; God bless this country.
