speakeroldname: Mr. Bernard Loiselle (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to participate in the Address in Reply to the Speech from the Throne, and I would like to join all those who have congratulated my two colleagues, the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Savard) and my colleague from Toronto (Mr. Robinson) who have been the first to speak in this debate. Mr. Speaker, I hope that this speech which I want to keep brief will allow me to correct certain figures, to set some facts in their true light, which will permit me to create the optimism that is necessary and that should normally flow from the situation prevailing in Canada.
A few weeks ago, as by-elections took place, I was personally involved in the riding of Saint-Hyacinthe. Mr. Speaker, I was surprised to see just how eager the opposition is to take power by any means, how they were prepared to use any argument without any basis in reality or on any economic fact. I see new members sitting on the opposite side of the House. Those new members are young people coming from all social classes, and I hope they will succeed in giving to the official opposition the desire to serve the cause at least by using sound and logical arguments which can be repeated throughout this country with the same conviction.
Mr. Speaker, we heard the Progressive Conservative candidate in Saint-Hyacinthe, probably as all or most of his other colleagues, saying that for one reason or another Canada had dropped from second to seventh rank-I do not know when- concerning the standard of living. Well, Mr. Speaker, that is absolutely false. Over the last ten years this country has recorded at all levels the best or the second best performance in the world.

October 30, 1978

We only have to look at the growth of employment from 1970 to 1977. The rate of growth in Canada was 23 per cent, followed by the United States with 15 per cent, then by Australia and Sweden-the latter being often cited as an example in Quebec-with 5 per cent. Japan, already cited as an example, also recorded 5 per cent. During the last decade, we have created around 250,000 new jobs a year. Mr. Speaker, you cannot find such a performance in any industrialized country during the last decade. As for growth of real domestic product, Canada ranked third with 4.5 per cent between 1968 and 1977. For the growth in industrial production, Canada had the second best percentage increase after Norway. In that country the rise was 38 per cent and 32 per cent in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I could go on putting up figures and a list of impressive statistics; they are not accidental but due to the rational and consistent economic policy of this government. I will not mention what happened before 1974 when I became a member of this House. But in 1974, when we compared our situation-including the unemployment rate-with that of our main trading partner, the United States, we could note that Canada was holding better in that period than its neighbours. But in 1975, things changed; our country had to cope with a very high inflation rate and a sudden increase in unemployment. In 1975, Mr. Speaker, before the government decided to come up with a price, wage and benefit control policy, the wage increase in Canada was approximately 22 per cent while the rise in productivity was only 2 per cent. During the same year, the increase in wages and productivity was respectively 9 and 5 per cent in the United States.
Germany, which is often quoted as an example, had a 7 per cent rate of wage increase and its rate of productivity increase was around 8 per cent. Mr. Speaker, our country, whose economy is above all based on exports, had to act and change the situation which prevailed in 1975.
Instead of the policy advocated by members opposite calling for a price and wage freeze for a given period, our Prime Minister preferred a policy of price and wage as well as profit control spread out over a period of more than three months. Of course, some members opposite are laughing. However, from the results of such a policy in the United States as well as in Britain, one realizes that now the advisers of the American president as well as the Britons would never revert to such a three-month policy which works to the disadvantage of the workers.
Mr. Speaker, the government did not simply decide to control prices and wages; it also decided in 1975 to use its own budget to decide and state that from now on the growth in government spending would not exceed that of the gross national product, namely the growth rate of our gross national product. This commitment on the part of the government has been respected, Mr. Speaker, and last August the Prime Minister intervened again and stated that from now on not only the growth rate of government spending would not exceed
The Address-Mr. B. Loiselle
the growth rate of the gross national product but would remain below it.
Mr. Speaker, it must also be noted that it is not merely by controlling government spending that the figures I stated earlier and several others which the Prime Minister referred to in his October 12 speech could be reached. Mr. Speaker, listening to the Tories during the last few months, you would have thought they had just discovered, after sitting down with a few Bay St. bankers and so-called businessmen, a series of new programs for economic recovery. We heard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) mention programs for small and medium businesses. We heard the Leader of the Opposition and also the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent) propose an over-all employment strategy, an industrial strategy for Canada.
We heard the Leader of the Opposition, during the summer months, put forward a series of programs, and I believe the only correlation that can be made is with the coldness of his feet at the thought of an election. Mr. Speaker, it is unbelievable! In the morning, the leader of the Conservative party would come up with plans to cut $5 to $6 billion off government spending, while in the afternoon and evening he would be promising new programs. You know, it is rather difficult to convince a serious audience, not a chamber of commerce but a fifth concession, which does not even exist anymore in Quebec, to convince them their taxes can be reduced on the one hand while new incentives given on the other. Mr. Speaker, how can you spend and save at the same time?
However, probably due to leaks from officials as suggested by the Prime Minister, they took and did a poor job of copying certain programs that have been in the making inside the government for more than two years.
Mr. Speaker, this is my second year as Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. When I assumed that responsibility last year, the department was already engaged in an analysis of our various industrial segments in Canada for more than a year. Our department developed during that period a specific diagnosis concerning the 23 main industrial segments. At the federal-provincial conference of ministers of industry, trade and commerce in February of last year, we discussed with each of the provincial ministers these diagnostic studies that had been made available to them some months before, and we put to them the following question: Do you agree or not with that diagnosis we are making of the economic situation in such or such an area? No province told us: No, we are not in total agreement. Each and everyone, including management, including labour, recognized the accurateness of all the facts in those studies. On the basis of those first talks between industry and commerce ministers and of subsequent discussions at the time of the federal-provincial conference of finance ministers as well as the conference of first ministers, Mr. Speaker, our government and, more particularly, our department created 23 task forces made up of provincial, management and union representatives

The Address-Mr. B. Loiselle
as well as, of course, some federal government members, in order that from that diagnosis we would be able to develop recommendations involving all participants and certain measures to correct situations where corrections were needed.
Mr. Speaker, for the first time in Canadian history, a government has clearly shown enough responsibility to convince both management and labour to sit around the same table and not only discuss in times of confrontation over the negotiation of labour contracts. They have been sitting together since last April to study the source of those problems and the corrective measures to take in each area.
Mr. Speaker, 850 recommendations have resulted from that serious work. On those 850 recommendations, some 400 are directed to the federal government. Mr. Speaker, when the Leader of the Opposition can only designate the hon. member-and it is strange he is not called Prime Minister anymore but the hon. member for Mount Royal-when the only word the members of the opposition can find when talking about this man is confrontation, but I shall come back to it when I get into constitutional matters, contrarily to the members opposite what they call confrontation is to me a good knowledge of the subject, which is completely different.
Mr. Speaker, I am talking about the process which started more than two years ago to demonstrate to what extent the government, confident in the economic situation, in the rules of the game, in the future of our country, committed itself with its partners of the economic sector to create not only a climate of optimism but also the climate that will encourage investors and that will encourage people not to be motivated by fear but by confidence in the economy and the future of their country.
Mr. Speaker, there are also other economic policies which unfortunately have not been reported adequately by the press. I refer to the statement made last May by the Minister of Public Works and Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Buchanan) when he set forth his policy on research and development. By this announcement, the federal government showed its willingness to appropriate 1.5 per cent of our gross national product for research and development.
The federal government introduced a series of incentives designed to urge Canadian firms to invest more in research and development so as to ensure a better co-ordination between the research conducted in universities and in the private sector, as well as to create jobs in the private sector for university graduates and the research field.
Mr. Speaker, all these policies make it possible today for a Canadian firm committed to research and development to pay

only about 20 cents for every dollar invested. Yet, Mr. Speaker, when we realize that after many years, and I make an exception for the ex-leader of the Conservative party (Mr. Stanfield), all the others propose a new R and D policy, it seems that R and D is something new for the Conservative party.
Mr. Speaker, there is another policy about which we said very little, that is our policy of assistance to small and medium-sized businesses as stated by the Minister of State (Small Business) (Mr. Abott) last June. That policy actually implemented many recommendations made by the president of the Association of Small and Medium-sized Businesses, Mr. Bullock. This is so true that a few weeks after our announcement, he wondered whether he was going to be asked to run as a Liberal candidate, and he would probably have been tempted to accept.
With the announcement of that policy, we agreed to tax rebates, we exempted from all federal taxes the first $50,000 of manufacturing production for each business, we agreed that family businesses, small and medium-sized, average their income over several years and be exempt from capital gains tax up to $200,000, if the business was sold to the children and grandchildren. In fact, we were accepting the major recommendations submitted by chambers of commerce, by pressure groups and particularly by Mr. Bullock's group.
Mr. Speaker, in August of this year, our government went a little further by announcing budget cuts to the tune of some $500 million for the current fiscal year, and of some $2 billion for the next one. Of course, there were members opposite who suggested that the Prime Minister had just become aware, that he had just discovered the way, a little like the third way in Quebec. If we made a mistake in the announcements we issued in August, it concerns not the accuracy of what we said but simply perhaps the form or format we chose. And I shall let the experts in communications pass judgment and do whatever analysis they require.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that our Prime Minister, no, I am not convinced, but I know for a fact that if our Prime Minister chose the month of August to announce a series of budgetary cuts after looking at the results of studies on the industrial sectors of Canada, after due consideration at the cabinet and subcommittee levels, and also in the Liberal caucus, it became clear that with the programs of industrial adjustment which had been studied by the cabinet, and approved in principle as for as their contents were concerned, it was necessary, because of their importance, to decide on further cuts elsewhere. With respect to the opposition members who have been announcing programs all through the summer, we know very well that they could only have picked them up from documents which some civil servants presumably fed up with the Liberals might have lost inadvertently. On that matter, as the Prime Minister said, there may be a lot more imagination in the critics raised by the Leader of the Opposition against us than in the quality of the programs that he developed by himself.

The Liberal party holds a record in the economic field which few other governments, amongst our neighbours, amongst industrialized countries, may boast of. This is evidenced by the fact that with a population of 23 million and a country like ours, we have been able to achieve the performances which are reflected in the statistics.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to deal with the constitutional issue, one which of course is at the centre of all discussions in the three-day period we are living now, the first day having ended at about six o'clock. Like most Canadians, I listened to the first reports of commentators and political experts who analysed the first day of discussions of the federal-provincial conference on the future of Canada and on the constitutional changes.
I have to admit, Mr. Speaker, that I am a little confused because I had to go by those reports because I was unable to listen to the speeches of all the provincial premiers. From bits and pieces of speeches and reports, especially those by Englishspeaking commentators, I had the impression that the Prime Minister had behaved like a perfect jackass throughout the day, that he had lacked leadership. But when we turned to the French channel, we heard someone say that the Prime Minister had been outstanding. So I think we will have to wait for the eleven o'clock news to have the story from both sides. However, from the little I have heard about what has been said today, one question comes to my mind: we had, gathered in this forum, the ten provincial premiers and the federal Prime Minister, that is the eleven Canadians who are or should be the most experienced men on matters related to the future, the possibilities and the constitutional changes to be made in this country.
Mr. Speaker, after witnessing the conduct of some, after listening to interviews given by some premiers, I wonder if they
The Address-Mr. B. Loiselle
realize that half of a country rests on the common will of its citizens and depends first and foremost on the choice of people of any language and culture to bring together their diversity, their skills, their heart and soul to live as a nation. The other half, Mr. Speaker, rests of course on economic and geographic reasons and one can prove, depending on the time and place, that reasons which were relevant ten years ago on economic grounds are less so today. But, Mr. Speaker, one thing that does not and will not change in any country of the world is the common desire to have a country and that desire is lacking in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, when one sees provincial premiers getting prepared for a conference in Regina to stonewall the federal government, one with natural resources, one with tariffs, another with off-shore resources and yet another using who knows what else, so they all say, like the Conservative leader, that they have come to a consensus, that they are all mad as hell. That Mr. Speaker, is the easiest thing to do. The problem is to arrive at some common denominator. The people from Alberta who are sitting here, my new friends whom I have learned to know since becoming a member of this House, there was a time when they needed the resources from the east to develop. Now it is us easterners who are asking them to show some heart and reason and help our economy. Indeed tomorrow if the wells dry up, they will have to live off their industrial development. Even the newly elected economists on the other side will not be able to deny such an obvious thruth.
Mr. Speaker, if we do not in this country define once and for all our willingness and reason for our staying together, or if we follow the Tory leader's philosophy and strip away most of the federal government's power, then I prefer being a separatist Quebecker. Because the day the federal government becomes a dead weight, Tory style-. What do you want, we might as well be Quebeckers, Ontarians, and westerners above all else. We will meet from time to time at the Calgary Stampede, but we will look after our own business. We would not thus take advantage of the benefit of the whole community because the country was made up of people who once shared common ideals, ideals of freedom and greatness throughout Canada, Mr. Speaker, ideals to build a country which would be envied by all humanists in the world. That challenge has been taken up by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who has been trying to explain it to us for the past ten years, but we refuse to budge. It would be more embarrassing to pass a bill of rights which would compel Canadians to show some openmindedness. Would it be more annoying for a premier of British Columbia who would not be much embarrassed if suddenly his fellow citizens wanted to vote against him as a result of the bill of rights? It would be better to restrict ourselves to a provincial charter as suggested by our premier, Mr. Levesque, but at least we know why he says so while we are not so sure about the others. However, Mr. Speaker, rather than enforce a bill of rights which would be included in that constitution as it is in most countries, we say: Let us have

However, Mr. Speaker, even Quebec separatists recognize that this country is useful for economic reasons. The proof is that they go on their knees to negotiate an economic partnership. And there are the other provinces; some of them assume a very proud attitude, but they will come to their senses sooner or later, and if Canada is a valid concept for economic reasons, Mr. Speaker, perhaps it is also a valid concept for humanitarian reasons or simply for the evolution of the human race.

I must confess, though, that that was so long ago that I have forgotten the details of what they said. A lot of water has flowed under
the bridge since then, but I do recall there was a lot more substance in their speeches than in the Speech from the Throne.
Indeed, it was a strange Speech from the Throne. And it has been a strange debate. The traditional approach is for the government to introduce by way of the Speech from the Throne its legislative agenda for the coming session. It lays out the plans it hopes to implement. The role of the opposition is to examine the government's proposals and to criticize them where they call for criticism. Members on the government side support the government. This time, though, we were given a completely vacuous Speech from the Throne. There was nothing in it, not a fresh idea. Then we had a speech from the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) containing positive proposals-

-while from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) we heard two full hours of criticism. We make no secret of the fact that we are practising to become the government, but I am surprised that the Prime Minister would demonstrate so openly that he was practising to be in opposition.
The Prime Minister proved again that he is a great Thespian, a great actor. He is long on style and short on substance. By a selective use of statistics he would have us believe that Canada's economy outperforms any other in the world. He sounded like someone from the Flat Earth Society trying to prove the world was flat. Nearly all the statistics he used were inaccurate, misleading or designed to disguise the truth. Since then a large number of editorialists and contributors to the media generally have drawn attention to this, while the results of the by-elections have shown that the voters had made that observation as well.
If our economy is performing better than any other in the world, as the Prime Minister would have us believe, why is our currency under such pressure? Why are people selling their Canadians dollars just as fast as they come into their hands? The Prime Minister would have us believe that Canadian dollars are the most coveted currency in the world because we have the strongest economy in the world. That is the kind of story he tries to tell us.
In his opening remarks the Prime Minister gave us a little psychology lesson. Recalling his earlier training, he said that the human mind has three facilities: memory, imagination and intelligence. He went on to demonstrate a very selective memory and a vivid imagination, and he tried to demonstrate that this House and this country lack the intelligence to see through his specious arguments. The great actor he is, he simply is not able to prove that the world is flat or that Canada's economy is out-performing the rest of the world.
I do not have the time to dwell on the many-faceted examples of misleading, total dishonesty and inaccurate information on the part of the Prime Minister in this debate. Nor do I have time to dwell on all of the reasons why the Trudeau government has mismanaged our economy. I want, rather, to deal with the questions which fall within my area of responsibility in this party, namely, the question of government spend-

October 30, 1978

ing and, in particular, government cutbacks. These subjects have been much in vogue lately.
This is a public issue. It started, I suppose, when the Prime Minister returned from Morocco. Prior to that, as a couple of people have indicated, he was "Schmidt-en" by the need to do something. He commandeered an hour or half an hour of prime time television and announced to the world that the government was going to cut back. He announced that to many of his ministers, who were quite surprised to find out that they were committed to take certain action about which they knew nothing. Then on September 8 we were given some details, finally, as to what these so-called cuts were supposed to be.
Since then we have seen some backing off on the part of many government departments, but the net result has been an escalation of public debate on government spending and on the amount of resources the government utilizes within our economy and, quite frankly, one of the most encouraging things which has happened recently has been the development of an attitude on the part of the population whereby people are sincerely and genuinely asking for less government.
Their voices are being heard. That is a position which my party and I have advocated for a long time, so naturally we feel encouraged by that sympathy for our view from the public.

Members of the New Democratic Party, of course, advocate just the opposite. They advocate more government, and I am sure that they feel that this view on the part of the public regarding less government, less involvement in the economy and less spending is a cosmic occurrence and a temporary aberration which will surely go away in time.
I do not think that is the reality of what is happening because it is evident to me, to people in my constituency, to people in other parts of the country and to people who have examined the record of the last decade, that governments cannot cure all problems. Over the last decade the view has been that any problem, be it economic or social, can be solved, given enough resources to be brought to bear and given good and well-motivated people with enough money. That was the approach which was taken, but it did not work. Government attempts over the last decade to redistribute income have, by and large, failed, as we have been reminded by the Council on Social Welfare here in Ottawa.
Governments over the last decade have taken on more and more responsibilities. They have been doing more and more, but they have not been doing well. The public is aware of that now and is very concerned about the lack of democratic control over spending. People have recognized that parliament has no control over the tax money which is being spent. People are now coming to appreciate that the cabinet has no control over the amount of money being spent. That is because of the style of the present Prime Minister, and it will change with a new prime minister next spring.
Part of this problem has to do with the sheer size of government and the resulting complexity. It is absolutely
The Address-Mr. Andre
important that we bring spending under control because, quite frankly, governments in Canada are now spending more money than the people are willing to provide. Empirical evidence for that is everywhere. Recently I read an article which knowledgeably estimated that the so-called underground economy in this country may account for 35 per cent of the total economy. Up to 35 per cent of the economy is being handled in a non-reportable and non-reported cash sense. People are using paper money. The barter system is being used to get beyond the reach of the tax collector. People resort to using hard cash as opposed to writing cheques and keeping books. They are doing that to avoid the tax assessor. People resort to barter because barter transactions are not taxable. They should be taxable, but cannot be traced.
Knowledgeable people estimate that these kinds of dealings may account for 35 per cent of our economy, and that figure is growing. That is a clear indication that a very large percentage of our population is simply unwilling to pay any more taxes. We cannot tax people more than they are willing to pay. Therefore, over an extended period of time governments cannot spend more than people are willing to pay.

The size and complexity of government means that large amounts of money will be spilled, and they are. A few days ago we were told that $142 million in UIC funds have been misspent. I think it was in the Montreal Gazette and I read an editorial today saying that that is only 4 per cent of all the funds handled by the UIC. It is a variation of the "what's a million" theme. It is only $142 million, but $142 million is a lot of money. Granted, it is only a small percentage of the whole, but it is a lot of money, and the individual Canadian taxpayer who might feel some conscience about seeking a tax avoidance scheme or who might not be paying taxes because he is engaging in underground economic activity finds that his qualms are dissipated immediately when he reads in the newspaper that the government has mismanaged UIC funds to that extent, when he reads that 16 per cent of civil servants are over-classified and therefore overpaid, that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) takes his friends to football games at a cost of $8,000, or reads about any of the assorted examples of government waste of taxpayers' money.
That has contributed substantially to this reluctance on the part of people to pay for government expenditures. The classic response to this circumstance of governments throughout history is to increase the number of tax collectors, and that is exactly what the Government of Canada has done. Between 1968 and 1977 the number of employees of the Department of National Revenue, the tax collectors of this country, went up from 15,500 to 23,600, a 52 per cent increase.
The money spent by government-the amount actually declared is 42 per cent of the gross national product-is not available to the private sector. It is not available for other productive purposes, and that is a reality. That is something we must face up to. Government spending is not productive. I am not saying it is not useful, but it is simply not productive. It

October 30, 1978
The Address-Mr. Andre
does not go into the generation of the goods and services which are part of our productive economy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They provide a service.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Of course they provide a service, but it is a service for which people are becoming unwilling to pay. A service is productive only if there is a customer who is willing to buy it, and when it costs 42 per cent of the gross national product, people become unwilling to pay for it. The evidence to substantiate that is everywhere.
Another effect of levying taxes beyond people's willingness to pay is a reduction in growth productivity. For example, an electrician who wants to build a rumpus room in his home for $6,000 might have to earn $10,000 pre-tax. If he builds it himself, it will cost $4,000 in materials. Therefore, he only needs to earn an additional $6,000 in order to have $4,000 after tax to do the job himself. The net result of that is that a carpenter loses $2,000 in salary, a net loss of revenue to the tax department of $2,000, and a loss of revenue to the government of $2,000.
Our present level of spending and taxation affects business decisions. Businessmen now make decisions on the basis of tax implications rather than other economic considerations. Investments are approached from the point of view of how much the tax load can be reduced by making an appropriate investment, rather than how it will affect the number of jobs and the growth of the company. After tax remuneration becomes the goal of people in unions and professions. Their goal is the actual amount they receive for the service performed. The service is immaterial; it is after tax remuneration which concerns them. Those pursuing that goal are stating categorically that they are unwilling to accept the tax load as part of their responsibility. The clear message is: they are unwilling to pay the taxes.
The other consequence of the disparity between government spending and people's willingness to pay is that it is impossible to reduce the deficit in a satisfactory manner. The raising of tax rates in order to raise more revenue is self-defeating. It results in less revenue. The people faced with the tax loads continue to borrow to finance the deficit. That merely results in greater problems for the future. There is the problem of having to pay back eventually and to sustain the interest charges and carrying costs on the borrowed funds.
Recently the country resorted to printing money as a policy option, which results in inflation. It offers temporary relief and growth in the economy, but over time it aggravates unemployment problems and causes serious consequences to the economy. The traditional Keynesian approaches of trying to spend oneself into prosperity do not work. We should address ourselves to this problem. We must close the gap between taxes and spending, working from both ends.
Another aspect of large government spending is the involvement of government in the economy and the effect of the sheer size of it. Last February the Minister of State (Small Busi-

ness) (Mr. Abbott) introduced the Paper Burden Office. He quoted statistics from an American study which indicated that the effective paperwork produced by the American government cost approximately $500 per citizen. Taking all levels of government into consideration, our government is larger on a per capita basis than that of the United States, and it is reasonable to assume that that estimate is equally applicable in this country. Indeed, the minister stated that it was his view that the indirect cost of government forcing people to fill out forms, apply for permits for every activity, take out licenses and react to the demands of government, is approximately $10 billion. That is the cost of the intrusions of big government into the private sector by way of the demands it makes. The present estimate is that Canadian governments account for 42 per cent of the gross national product. If the indirect costs of government are added on, which cost is imposed upon our economy, and if government tax is defined as all expenditures resulting from government action, then surely it is obvious governments are responsible for far more than 50 per cent of the g.n.p. in a direct and indirect sense.
Indeed government spending is one of the most crucial problems we must address ourselves to if the economy is to work in the 1980s, and if the one million unemployed are to be put to work. There appears to be a public will in Canada to support endeavours to find ways to reduce the over-all level of spending. The Liberal party has been true to its flexible principles, has acknowledged its view in public, and apparently has launched itself on a path of reduced government expenditures. I say "apparently" because a lot was said on August 1 and September 8 which was not factual.
On September 8 the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) announced the details of spending cuts. Included were cuts to the Farm Credit Corporation of $23 million, to CMCH of $200 million, to the Export Development Corporation of $240 million, to the Federal Business Development Bank of $22 million, and under the Public Utilities Income Tax Transfer Act of $49 million. The supposed cuts totalled $534 million. They were not cuts at all, they were bookkeeping changes. The government indicated to the Farm Credit Corporation, CMHC, Export Development Corporation and others that they would not receive capital advances from the Department of Finance, but that they would have to go to the market and borrow those funds directly.
Because of that, these entries no longer appear in the blue book estimates which we receive each year. They no longer appear as government spending, and they are claimed to be cuts. They are no such thing. They represent no change in the operations of Crown corporations; they represent a change in the bookkeeping entries. If a private company attempted to make such changes in its accounting practices, it would be called to task by the stock exchange. The tax deductions claimed by a similar method for this current fiscal year amounted to over $1 billion. They were nothing but bookkeeping or accounting changes. They had nothing to do with cuts whatsoever.

The danger cannot be underestimated. The electorate will not be fooled because we will make sure they are informed. The danger is that too many people and organizations accept government figures as fact. In its latest report the Economic Council of Canada accepted the Treasury Board statements of government spending as fact. Those were the figures which they applied in order to arrive at recommendations for the future. Those numbers are wrong because the basis of determination has been changed. The government has disguised some of its spending. When the Economic Council of Canada and others engaged in the business of analysing our economy use numbers which are produced by the Treasury Board as true and factual estimates of government spending, they use the wrong data because the bases are changing from year to year. So they are bound to reach the wrong conclusions.
I think it behooves me in the last five minutes, and I will not be long, to outline briefly what can and should be done. First and foremost, in order truly to bring government spending under control and to bring growth level to a reasonable point, we must have more honesty and openness about government spending. This is not a unique or original idea. That is part of a recommendation of the C. D. Howe Research Institute policy analysis and report of 1975. Three years ago that institute recognized that one of the key contributors to this tremendous increase in government spending could be related to the government's not being honest and open about its programs and plans. This is an absolutely essential first step to providing control in respect of government spending.
We have many examples of the things governments are doing. We must examine some of the things governments are doing in order to determine if in fact the private sector could not be doing those same things, to see if in fact there could not be some rationalization, and to see whether some activities in which the government is now engaged, and perhaps has been engaged properly so in the past, should no longer be done by the government.
I am reminded of a story of a few years ago which illustrates the point I am trying to make. Someone examined the public accounts and discovered that the Department of Agriculture was making an annual grant to a horse racing stable owned by E. P. Taylor, a man of some means. Someone asked why E. P. Taylor, a very wealthy man, was receiving a grant from the Department of Agriculture. It turned out this was being done under an old program established in 1910, or thereabouts, to permit the development of better cavalry horses. Fortunately that program was brought to an end.

I wonder how many more such examples there are on the books. I am sure there are many. The proposal of this party is that we institute a sunset law under which all programs of government would automatically be subjected to a detailed and thorough review on a regular basis. There are
The Address-Mr. Andre
scores of things governments are doing which in the first instance were very appropriate for governments to do, but which are now no longer appropriate and in fact should be turned over to the private sector. I am sure that among the 384 Crown corporations, at last count-and probably there are more than 400 now because the number is increasing at a rate of three a month-we could find some whose activities could either be discontinued or turned over to the private sector.
I think it is about time we assessed the real indirect costs of government, an example of which is the $10 billion resulting from the government putting demands upon the private sector. A sneaky thing which has been happening recently, and which is of great concern, is the way in which governments have been imposing additional costs. One example comes to mind regarding drilling in the high Arctic. The Department of the Environment, for good and valid reasons, has said that prior to such drilling the companies must conduct environmental assessments. There is good and valid reason for that, but that involves a cost; in essence a tax. No one has done a cost-benefit analysis of that requirement to determine whether the benefits achieved from that expenditure are in fact worth the effort. That is just one of scores of examples.
What the United States terms "deregulation" is a policy that must certainly be adopted in this country. We must engage in systematic deregulation and an examination of the demands the government makes upon the private sector. We must make a systematic check of the tests, permits and licensing policies which now exist. All these things should be subjected to a cost benefit analysis in order that we can determine whether the benefits produced are in excess of the cost.
We must also restore democratic control over spending. The former leader of my party, the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield), made an excellent address about a year and a half or two years ago to Mount Allison University regarding the dangers to our democracy of a continuation of the type of growth we have experienced in recent years. If we are so shortsighted as not to recognize the potential dangers, so eloquently articulated by the hon. member, then we will be shortchanging our successors, our children and their children, to a very great degree. Because what we will be leaving them by way of a legacy will not be democratic, or a parliamentary democracy of the type we now know. Thus, we must give parliament more control over government spending. We must have more honesty from government in respect of spending and taxation, and we simply must stop deceiving the public. After I heard the news that the Prime Minister was not going to call an election, I thought that surely to God there would be something dynamic in the Speech from the Throne, that it would be laden with positive, fighting economic and social measures to get this country moving again.
I am sure hon. members opposite would say that I have been around here too long, and they are not going to like what I am about to say, and that is that if that was not the worst throne speech I have heard in my 20 years, I will eat my hat. It was easily the worst, the damndest document of generalities, at a time when the Canadian people were looking for leadership and positive economic measures to get the economy going; but instead the four million to five million low income people of Canada have been kicked once again. Canadians were looking for social legislation that had some meaning, but what did they get? They got the most general motherhood document I have ever seen in my life. Can anyone name me one significant thing outlined in that document-just one? I certainly did not hear any named during the throne debate either, because there was nothing to name.
Hon. members opposite are going to say, "Wait for our positive legislative package that is to be brought forward independent of that throne speech." It was not really a throne speech in the true tradition of the throne speech. I can think of past Liberal governments that were really serious vis-a-vis socioeconomic legislation, but 1 am sure that members opposite are going to have a pretty good time defending this document.
We are now told by the leader of the government to wait for the legislative package. I respectfully submit that no matter what the package is going to be in the weeks and months ahead, it will be too late to have any real, concrete effect at the grass roots level, because of the mess that this worst government since confederation has plunged the country into. The record is there-a fallen dollar, one million unemployed and inflation. Has there ever a worse economic situation?
As I said earlier, the Prime Minister has said that the country is divided today as it has never been divided before. Where have members opposite been for the last ten years, sitting complacently on their hands and doing nothing?
